Autoxide documentation v0.20.0

Autoxide

English · Tiếng Việt

Autoxide is an open-source backend core written in Rust. The core is built first; business modules plug in on top of it. It runs on both SQLite and PostgreSQL from a single code base, exposes a REST API described by OpenAPI, and is designed to be used by AI agents as well as by people.

It is a foundation for new products. It is not tied to any company or industry: the core contains no business concepts — those belong to modules.

A commerce-ready backend for the Vietnamese market. Taxes (a dated tax data pack), accounting documents and invoices, the official list of administrative units for addresses and the legal rules (e-commerce, personal data, record keeping) come built in. AI agents use it through MCP and the OpenAPI contract, with the same permissions as people. The core stays neutral and modules plug in. Payment, SMS, shipping and e-invoice providers sit behind interfaces that ship today with simulated providers only: connecting a real provider is still to be done.

Try it in one command

Just looking around? autoxide demo needs no setup: it creates a folder, a SQLite database, random secrets and an administrator, loads the reference data, and prints the administrator’s password on screen. The API reference opens at /api/docs. Not for production.

# With Docker (nothing to install or compile):
docker run --rm -it -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 ghcr.io/thuongtamduy/autoxide:latest demo
# Or with a downloaded binary (Linux, macOS, Windows: see the release page):
./autoxide demo

Needs a release made after 0.19.0. docs/GETTING-STARTED.md has the downloads, keeping the demo data, and the next steps.

Quickstart

One command, nothing to compile: SQLite in a Docker volume, the tables created, a first administrator and the reference data loaded. You need Docker (with Compose) and openssl.

mkdir autoxide && cd autoxide
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thuongtamduy/autoxide/main/compose.quickstart.yml
# Two secrets, kept in .env next to it (never commit it)
printf 'AUTOXIDE_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET=%s\nAUTOXIDE_SECRET_KEY=%s\n' \
  "$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr -d '\n')" "$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr -d '\n')" > .env

docker compose -f compose.quickstart.yml up -d
# The administrator's generated password (see below)
docker compose -f compose.quickstart.yml exec autoxide autoxide initial-password

The first administrator’s password. On its first start the server creates the administrator admin@example.com with a generated password. The password never goes to the log (logs are often collected elsewhere): it is written once to the file data/initial-admin-password, which only the server’s user can read. Inside the container that is /var/lib/autoxide/data/initial-admin-password, in the Docker volume data (named <directory>_data by Compose), so it survives restarts. The command above prints its two lines: the email, then the password. The log only says where the file is (docker compose -f compose.quickstart.yml logs autoxide | grep "first administrator"). If the command says the file “does not exist”, an administrator existed already (the volume was used before), or you set AUTOXIDE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD yourself. Once you have signed in and changed the password, delete the file: docker compose -f compose.quickstart.yml exec autoxide autoxide initial-password --remove.

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8080/ (name, version and links) and sign in. The API reference page (/api/docs, it loads its script from a CDN) is off in the quickstart: add AUTOXIDE_HTTP_API_DOCS=true to .env and run docker compose -f compose.quickstart.yml up -d again to turn it on.

curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"<the password from the file>"}'

The guides in docs/guides/ write the same request shorter with --json '…', which needs curl 7.82 or newer (curl --version); with an older curl, write -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '…' instead.

To choose them yourself, add AUTOXIDE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL=… and AUTOXIDE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=… to .env before the first start. Next: connect an AI agent over MCP (docs/guides/mcp.md). The quickstart needs a release made after 0.16.0; for PostgreSQL, several servers and HTTPS, see docs/DEPLOY.md.

What the quickstart contains

The released image contains every module of the autoxide binary (all of modules/ except the sample notes). The server runs the core and official ones by default; the experimental ones (marked * below) are off until you name them in AUTOXIDE_MODULES — see docs/MODULES.md for the tiers and how to choose. GET /api/v1/kernel/modules lists what runs on your server. Each module answers under /api/v1/<module>.

AreaModules
Accounts and accessauth (sign-in, roles, API keys, two-step sign-in, passkeys), organizations (tenants, units, stores), audit, idempotency
Platformfiles, mail, notifications, webhooks, ai (off until you configure a provider), address (Vietnamese administrative units), compliance, plans (plans and subscriptions), reporting*, automations*
Websitecontent (posts, pages), media, menus, forms, newsletter*, comments*, analytics*
Commercecatalog, inventory, promotions, shipping, orders, customers, tax, ledger (money), invoices
Servicebookings*, support*, conversations*

Nothing has to be turned on to try the core and official modules, and a module whose data you never write costs nothing. Modules that talk to outside services (an AI provider, payment or shipping partners, SMTP) send nothing out until you configure them. Which modules each tenant may use is set by its plan (docs/PLANS.md); the set the server runs is chosen with AUTOXIDE_MODULES (docs/MODULES.md), and listing it needs the kernel.modules.read permission (the administrator has it).

Changing a record: If-Match

Reading one record returns its version in the ETag header. Send it back in If-Match when you change the record, so two people never overwrite each other: a stale version gets 412, and endpoints that require the header answer 428 without it.

# Read the post and keep its ETag header (a quoted number, such as "1763700000000000")
curl -sS -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/content/entries/<id> -H 'Authorization: Bearer <access token>'
# Change it with that ETag
curl -sS -X PATCH http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/content/entries/<id> \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <access token>' -H 'If-Match: <the ETag>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"A new title"}'

docs/guides/errors.md shows each answer (428, 412) as a run example.

Status

The core is complete: every step of the roadmap is done — project skeleton, foundation, login with roles and permissions, two-step sign-in, events and audit log, job queue, i18n and idempotency, email, file storage, MCP endpoint, sample module, tooling and deployment, passkeys, session management, account deletion and data export, webhooks. Business modules come next. The core has the Cargo workspace, the quality gate, configuration, database access, per-module migrations, the module contract, the HTTP server under /api/v1 with OpenAPI, health checks, logs, metrics, tracing and the CLI. The auth module stores users with Argon2id password hashes and signs them in with short-lived access tokens and rotating refresh tokens (/api/v1/auth/login, /refresh, /logout, /me). Access is controlled by roles: each module declares its permissions, roles group them (/api/v1/auth/roles), and a built-in admin role has them all. The first administrator is created from the command line (autoxide user create); after that, administrators manage accounts through /api/v1/auth/users. People can create their own accounts only when AUTOXIDE_AUTH_SELF_REGISTRATION=true. Programs and AI agents use API keys (/api/v1/auth/api-keys): a key acts as the user who created it, limited to the permissions listed on it, and is sent like an access token (Authorization: Bearer axk1_…; the key names its tenant, so no other header is needed). Creating a key, like adding a passkey, asks for the user’s current password, and resetting a password removes every key and passkey of that account. Users can turn on two-step sign-in with an authenticator app (TOTP) and get one-time recovery codes (/api/v1/auth/me/mfa). Every change is kept in an append-only audit log — who, what, which record, when, before and after — readable at /api/v1/audit with the audit.read permission. Background jobs live in the database too (no Redis): retried with backoff, kept when they fail for good (autoxide jobs failed, autoxide jobs retry), and run on a schedule when a module asks. AUTOXIDE_PROCESS_ROLE splits a deployment into API processes and worker processes. Error messages come in English or Vietnamese, chosen with the Accept-Language header. Write requests sent with an Idempotency-Key header are safe to retry: a repeat returns the first result (except a result holding a one-time secret, such as a new API key, which is never stored: the repeat gets 409 idempotency_result_not_kept). Mail goes out through SMTP from the job queue (password reset, email verification). Files are stored on local disk or in S3. AI agents call the system as tools over MCP at /mcp, read its resources (module guides, JSON Schemas) and prompts, and find their way from /llms.txt, a page generated from the code.

What the core contains, in build order (see docs/ROADMAP.md):

  1. Foundation: configuration, database access, migrations per module, the module contract, one error type, HTTP under /api/v1, OpenAPI, health checks, logs, metrics, tracing, CLI
  2. Login, roles and permissions, API keys for machines and AI agents
  3. MFA (TOTP and recovery codes)
  4. Events and an append-only audit log
  5. A job queue stored in the database (no Redis)
  6. i18n (English, Vietnamese) and idempotency keys
  7. Email, password reset, email verification
  8. File storage (local disk and S3)
  9. An MCP endpoint so AI agents can call the system as tools
  10. A sample module and a guide for writing modules
  11. Tooling and deployment: data copy between SQLite and PostgreSQL, benchmarks, Docker, backup and restore, a one-command check (./gate.sh)
  12. Passkeys; 13–14. account management, webhooks, a hardened API contract
  13. A media library: images, video, audio and documents in nested folders, served publicly or privately (docs/MEDIA.md)
  14. Content: posts and pages in several languages, drafts and history, scheduling, categories, tags, authors, menus, redirects, and public endpoints for the website (docs/CONTENT.md)
  15. AI features, off by default, with the provider you choose (Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Ollama…): SEO and alt text suggestions, translation into drafts, search by meaning, and permissions that keep AI agents to their own work (docs/AI.md)
  16. Forms: contact and sign-up forms defined through the API, answers checked on the server, spam held back, an inbox with CSV export (docs/FORMS.md)
  17. Newsletters: lists, double opt-in, one-click unsubscribe, campaigns sent in batches with pause and resume, bounces, mail for new posts (docs/NEWSLETTER.md)
  18. Comments: two-level comments on any target for signed-in users or guests, a fixed moderation pipeline, reports, bans, reply mails (docs/COMMENTS.md)
  19. Website menus: main bar, mega menus and footer whose items link to addresses or to objects of any module, with automatic sub-items, dated badges and a cached public endpoint (docs/MENUS.md)
  20. Organizations and identity: an organization tree in each tenant (head office, regions, stores…) with permissions scoped to a unit or a branch, settings inherited down the tree, a website per unit, public store profiles; customer accounts apart from staff, invitations, sign-in links, delegation down chains of tenants, time-limited support access; the official list of Vietnamese administrative units for addresses (docs/ADDRESS.md)

Try it with Docker (no build)

The same as the Quickstart, step by step with plain docker run (works with every release): nothing to compile, SQLite inside a Docker volume. You need Docker and openssl. The image is about 410 MB on disk and the server is ready about a second after it starts.

# Two secrets, made up here and kept in a file (use the same ones on every start; never commit it)
printf 'AUTOXIDE_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET=%s\nAUTOXIDE_SECRET_KEY=%s\n' \
  "$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr -d '\n')" "$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr -d '\n')" > autoxide.env
chmod 600 autoxide.env

IMAGE=ghcr.io/thuongtamduy/autoxide:0.20.0   # a release from the GitHub Releases page
RUN="docker run --rm --env-file autoxide.env -v autoxide-data:/var/lib/autoxide/data"

# 1. Create the tables (the server will not start before this, and again after every update)
$RUN $IMAGE migrate up
# 2. The first administrator: a strong password is printed once
$RUN $IMAGE user create --email you@example.com --name "Your Name" --admin
# 3. Reference data (addresses, taxes, promotion limits); each is safe to run again
$RUN $IMAGE task address.import
$RUN $IMAGE task tax.import_pack
$RUN $IMAGE task promotions.load_legal_data
# 4. Start the server (it listens inside the container; this publishes it on this machine only)
docker run -d --name autoxide --restart unless-stopped --env-file autoxide.env \
  -v autoxide-data:/var/lib/autoxide/data -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 $IMAGE serve

curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/health/ready     # {"data":{"status":"ok"}}
$RUN $IMAGE doctor                           # what is still missing before going live

Keep -v autoxide-data:/var/lib/autoxide/data on every command: the database, uploaded files and mail live in that volume, and without it they vanish with the container. A backup must go to a directory you mount, not to a path inside the container (mkdir backups && sudo chown 10001 backups, then add -v "$PWD/backups:/backups" and run backup /backups/<name>). Sign in as shown under Configuration (use http://127.0.0.1:8080). For PostgreSQL, a reverse proxy with HTTPS, updates and restore, see docs/DEPLOY.md.

No Docker? Build the binary and run it by hand: docs/DEPLOY.md, section B (SQLite) or B+ (PostgreSQL). The two secrets go in .env, autoxide migrate up runs before autoxide serve, and AUTOXIDE_HTTP_ADDRESS changes the address.

Requirements

These are only needed to build from source (to run a released image, see above).

  • Rust — rustup installs the exact toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml the first time you run cargo
  • A C compiler (SQLite and libwebp are compiled from source and bundled into the binary; on Debian or Ubuntu: sudo apt install build-essential)
  • To run the full quality gate: Docker and cargo-deny (cargo install cargo-deny --locked)

Building takes a while. The first build (cargo build --release, or docker build) compiles several hundred crates: count on roughly 20 minutes to well over an hour, depending on the number of CPU cores and the memory (at least 4 GB of RAM, 8 GB is comfortable; raise Docker Desktop’s memory limit if a build is killed). Later builds reuse what was compiled. To run Autoxide rather than change it, use the released image above: nothing to compile.

Behind a company proxy. cargo and rustup read HTTPS_PROXY (and HTTP_PROXY, NO_PROXY) from the environment. docker build does not pass your shell’s variables into the build: give them as build arguments, which Docker knows already and does not keep in the image —

docker build --build-arg HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:3128   --build-arg HTTP_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:3128 --build-arg NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1   -t autoxide .

— or set them once under proxies in ~/.docker/config.json, which Docker passes to every build, docker compose build included. A proxy that inspects HTTPS with its own certificate makes the downloads fail with certificate errors inside the build; use the released image then.

Getting started

git clone https://github.com/thuongtamduy/autoxide.git autoxide
cd autoxide

# Build and run the command-line interface
cargo run -p autoxide -- --help

# Run the tests on SQLite (no setup needed)
cargo test --workspace

# Run the full quality gate: format, lints, boundary checks, dependency audit,
# tests on SQLite, tests on PostgreSQL (started in a throwaway Docker container)
./gate.sh

If you are going to commit, enable the Git hooks once. They scan staged changes for secrets (when gitleaks is installed) and check formatting:

git config core.hooksPath .githooks

Configuration

Every setting has a working default, so a fresh clone runs without any configuration. Settings are read from environment variables and from a .env file in the current directory; environment variables win.

# Check the configuration and show every setting with its current value
cargo run -p autoxide -- config

# Start your own configuration from the documented defaults
cp .env.example .env

The database schema is managed by migrations, one set per module. They are never applied automatically — run them once per deployment:

cargo run -p autoxide -- migrate status          # what is applied, what is pending
cargo run -p autoxide -- migrate up              # apply everything that is pending
cargo run -p autoxide -- migrate down <module>   # revert the newest migration of one module

Create the first administrator. A strong password is generated and printed once; to choose your own, pipe it in and add --password-stdin:

cargo run -p autoxide -- user create --email you@example.com --name "Your Name" --admin

Import the reference data the server ships with. No step changes your own data, and running one again changes nothing:

# The Vietnamese administrative units (provinces, communes), used to check addresses.
# Nothing imports it for you: run it once per installation, and again when an update
# ships a newer list (`doctor` says so). See docs/ADDRESS.md.
cargo run -p autoxide -- task address.import

# The tax data pack (rates, withholding rules). A running server imports it by itself
# within an hour; run this to have it at once. See docs/TAX.md.
cargo run -p autoxide -- task tax.import_pack

# The legal limits on promotions (Vietnam). Without them promotions cannot be turned on
# (`doctor` warns). See docs/PROMOTIONS.md.
cargo run -p autoxide -- task promotions.load_legal_data

Check the installation. doctor goes through the configuration, the database, the migrations, the signing keys, file storage, the SMTP server, the administrator account and the imported reference data, and says how to fix each problem (--json for scripts and AI agents; it exits with status 1 when a check failed):

cargo run -p autoxide -- doctor

Modules can add maintenance tasks; autoxide task lists them with their arguments (cargo run -p autoxide -- task).

Then start the server. It refuses to start while a migration is pending, and stops gracefully on Ctrl-C or SIGTERM (requests in progress get AUTOXIDE_HTTP_SHUTDOWN_SECONDS to finish; behind a load balancer, see updating without dropping requests):

cargo run -p autoxide -- serve

By default it listens on 127.0.0.1:8080: check it with curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/health/ready. Logs go to standard error. Sign in and look at your account:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email": "you@example.com", "password": "<the password>"}'
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/auth/me -H 'Authorization: Bearer <access_token>'

The API contract is an OpenAPI document generated from the code. It is committed as docs/openapi.json, printed by autoxide openapi, and served by the running server at /api/v1/openapi.json. Its description lists the conventions every endpoint follows (response envelope, RFC 9457 errors with a stable code, cursor pagination, request ids).

AI agents reach the same functions as tools through the Model Context Protocol at /mcp (Streamable HTTP), authenticated like the API — an API key is the usual choice. An agent sees and calls only the tools its permissions allow; each tool runs the same code as the matching REST endpoint, so writes land in the audit log. For example, with Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http autoxide http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer <api key>"

docs/guides/mcp.md walks through it: a key with the least permissions, other MCP clients, every tool with the permission it needs, and the limits.

Back up everything — the data of every module and every stored file — into a directory, and restore it into a new, empty database (with any file storage) later. The database is read in one consistent snapshot, so the server may keep running:

cargo run -p autoxide -- backup backups/2026-11-11
cargo run -p autoxide -- restore backups/2026-11-11

Restore only backups you made yourself: a backup is the whole content of the server.

To move to PostgreSQL later (or bring data back to SQLite), stop the server and copy everything into a new, empty database; it gets every migration first:

printf '%s' 'postgres://user:password@host:5432/autoxide' | cargo run -p autoxide -- copy --to-stdin

.env.example lists every setting with its description and default. It is generated from the code, so it cannot go out of date. An invalid configuration is reported in full — every problem at once, each saying what to fix — and the command exits with status 2. Secrets are never printed.

Each client address may make 600 requests a minute by default (AUTOXIDE_HTTP_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE), and an email is locked for 15 minutes after 5 failed sign-ins. Behind a reverse proxy, set AUTOXIDE_HTTP_CLIENT_IP_HEADER (for example to X-Forwarded-For) so that clients are told apart by their own address rather than the proxy’s.

Users can also sign in with a passkey (Face ID, fingerprint, security key) instead of a password. Set AUTOXIDE_AUTH_PASSKEY_RP_ID to your site’s domain (and AUTOXIDE_AUTH_PASSKEY_ORIGINS when your web app runs on a subdomain); a signed-in user adds one with POST /api/v1/auth/me/passkeys/registration and POST /api/v1/auth/me/passkeys, and signs in with POST /api/v1/auth/login/passkey/options and POST /api/v1/auth/login/passkey — no email needed. The options returned go straight to PublicKeyCredential.parseCreationOptionsFromJSON() / parseRequestOptionsFromJSON() in the browser.

Signing in with Google, Microsoft, GitHub or any OpenID Connect provider is off by default; turn it on with AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OIDC=true, then each tenant adds its providers with POST /api/v1/auth/oidc-providers (permission auth.oidc.manage). An existing account is linked only when both sides have verified the email, and two-step sign-in still applies. See docs/guides/oidc.md.

Users with the files.upload permission upload a file by sending its raw content to POST /api/v1/files?name=report.pdf with its Content-Type, then list, download (GET /api/v1/files/{id}/content) and delete their own files; files.manage reaches everyone’s. Uploads are limited to 25 MiB (AUTOXIDE_FILES_MAX_BYTES) and, when you set AUTOXIDE_FILES_ALLOWED_TYPES (for example image/*,application/pdf), to those media types.

Uploaded files are stored in data/files until you set AUTOXIDE_FILES_S3_BUCKET (with AWS_REGION, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL for an S3-compatible service such as Cloudflare R2). Back up data/files together with the database.

Mail is written as .eml files to data/mail until you set AUTOXIDE_MAIL_SMTP_URL (for example smtps://user:password@smtp.example.com:465) and AUTOXIDE_MAIL_FROM.

A user who forgot their password calls POST /api/v1/auth/password-reset with their email and receives a one-time token by mail, valid for 30 minutes; they then call POST /api/v1/auth/password-reset/confirm with the token and a new password. The answer is the same whether or not the email has an account. Set AUTOXIDE_AUTH_PASSWORD_RESET_URL (for example https://app.example.com/reset?token={token}) to send a link to your own page instead of the bare token.

Signed-in users change their own password with POST /api/v1/auth/me/password (the current password is required). An administrator can give the first password to an account created without one (PUT /api/v1/auth/users/{id}/password), but cannot replace a password someone already has.

Each sign-in is a session, named by the session_id in the token response. Users see their sessions — device and last activity — at GET /api/v1/auth/me/sessions, sign one out with DELETE /api/v1/auth/me/sessions/{id}, or every other one with DELETE /api/v1/auth/me/sessions?keep={their session_id}. Users download everything the server keeps about them with GET /api/v1/auth/me/export and delete their account with DELETE /api/v1/auth/me (current password required); every module then deletes its data about them. Administrators find users with GET /api/v1/auth/users?search=ada, sign a user out everywhere (DELETE /api/v1/auth/users/{id}/sessions) and delete accounts (DELETE /api/v1/auth/users/{id}). An administrator cannot act this way on someone who holds permissions they lack.

Other systems receive events through webhooks: with the webhooks.manage permission, register an https:// address and the events it wants at POST /api/v1/webhooks (the list of events is at GET /api/v1/webhooks/events). Each event is sent as a signed POST following Standard Webhooks, so the receiver can check it with an existing library and the secret returned at creation. Failed deliveries are retried for about two hours; GET /api/v1/webhooks/{id}/deliveries shows what was sent and what failed. Webhooks go only to public addresses: an address in a private or local network (localhost, 10.x, 192.168.x, 169.254.x…) is refused, unless AUTOXIDE_WEBHOOKS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_NETWORKS=true because the receivers run in your own network.

New accounts receive a mail asking to confirm their address; the token in it (valid 24 hours) is confirmed with POST /api/v1/auth/email-verification/confirm, and email_verified_at then shows when. To change their email, users call POST /api/v1/auth/me/email with the new address and their password: the email changes only once the new address is confirmed the same way. The old address then gets a mail saying so, with a token (valid 7 days) to report a change the owner did not make: POST /api/v1/auth/email-change/report signs the account out everywhere, removes its password, passkeys, API keys and two-step sign-in, gives the old address back when it is still free, and sends a password-reset mail there. Set AUTOXIDE_AUTH_EMAIL_VERIFICATION_URL and AUTOXIDE_AUTH_EMAIL_CHANGE_REPORT_URL to link these mails to your own pages.

For production, set AUTOXIDE_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET (the key that signs access tokens) to a long random value, the same on every server:

openssl rand -base64 48

Without it the server makes up a key at startup and logs a warning: fine for trying Autoxide out, but signed-in clients must refresh their access token after every restart.

Running the tests against your own PostgreSQL

Tests pick their database from TEST_DATABASE_URL. Unset means SQLite. To use PostgreSQL 16 or newer, point it at any database on a server where the user may CREATE DATABASE — every test creates its own empty database and drops it afterwards:

TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/postgres cargo test --workspace

./gate.sh does this for you with Docker. To make the gate use an existing server instead, set GATE_POSTGRES_URL to the same kind of URL.

Tests that build the whole application copy a template database that already has every migration applied, instead of migrating each empty database again. The templates live in the system temporary directory (autoxide-templates/) and, on PostgreSQL, as databases named autoxide_tpl_…; both are rebuilt when the test program or its migrations change, and removed after an hour. Set TEST_DATABASE_TEMPLATE=off to migrate every test database from scratch.

File storage tests also run against S3 when TEST_S3_ENDPOINT points at an S3-compatible service with a bucket named autoxide-test. The gate starts a throwaway S3 emulator (moto) in Docker for this; set GATE_S3_ENDPOINT to use an existing service instead.

Project layout

PathWhat it is
crates/kernelThe foundation every module builds on. Knows no module.
crates/appThe autoxide binary: the one place where modules are registered.
crates/testkitTest support: an isolated database per test, on SQLite or PostgreSQL.
modules/<name>One crate per module, each owning its tables (auth accounts and sign-in, audit, files, mail, webhooks, content, media, catalog, orders… — about thirty; ls modules lists them, the sections above say what each does).
xtaskDeveloper tooling: cargo xtask check enforces the workspace boundaries.
gate.shThe quality gate. A change is done only when this is green.

Modules own their tables, talk to each other only through published traits, and never share foreign keys. These rules are checked automatically by the gate.

Documentation

  • STACK.md — which libraries are used and why
  • docs/ROADMAP.md — what is built, in what order
  • docs/decisions/ — the decision log (the old entries are in docs/DECISIONS.md, new ones one file each here); cargo xtask decisions generates a by-topic index, INDEX.md, that is not committed
  • CLAUDE.md — the rules for contributors, human or AI agent
  • CHANGELOG.md — what changed in each release; released Docker images are at ghcr.io/<owner>/autoxide
  • docs/COMPATIBILITY.md — what stays stable from 1.0 (API, error codes, settings, migrations, the Rust API for modules) and what may change
  • docs/guides/ — task-by-task guides to the API, with curl and TypeScript examples that run as tests: a website, signing in, API keys, retries, pagination, errors, connecting an AI agent over MCP
  • sdk/typescript/ — a typed TypeScript client generated from docs/openapi.json; docs/mcp-tools.json — the contract of every MCP tool
  • docs/DEPLOY.md — installing and deploying: Docker Compose with PostgreSQL or one binary with SQLite, reverse proxy, updates, backups
  • docs/MEDIA.md — using the media library: upload, folders, public links, caching, trash
  • docs/CONTENT.md — using the content module: drafts, publishing, pages and addresses, languages, public endpoints for the website, preview
  • docs/AI.md — the AI features: turning them on with each provider, embeddings, costs and limits, what is sent, limits for AI agents
  • docs/FORMS.md — using the forms module: defining a form, showing it on a website, anti-spam, the inbox, data requests by email
  • docs/NEWSLETTER.md — using the newsletter module: lists, the website’s sign-up, confirmation and preferences pages, campaigns, bounces, legal notes
  • docs/COMMENTS.md — using the comments module: targets, the website’s thread and comment box, moderation, reports and bans, reply mails, legal notes
  • docs/MENUS.md — using the menus module: items, objects of other modules, badges, the public endpoint and its caching, moving from the content module’s menus
  • docs/BOOKINGS.md — bookings: services, staff and rooms, weekly schedules in the unit’s time zone, free times, deposits through the payment partner, cancellation policy, reminders, guests with a phone code
  • docs/CUSTOMERS.md — customers: profiles by account or phone number, purchase history from orders, masked contact details with audited reveal, manual and rule groups
  • docs/SUPPORT.md — customer support tickets: guests with a ticket token, staff scope by unit, teams and routing, business-hour deadlines, hand-over to consumer complaints, AI drafts
  • docs/ANALYTICS.md — cookieless website analytics: sending events from a website, reports, funnels, consent for per-person tracking, legal notes
  • docs/ADDRESS.md — administrative units and addresses: reading the list, importing the official list
  • docs/CATALOG.md — products: variants, categories, price lists with history, price floors
  • docs/PROMOTIONS.md — promotions: automatic discounts, coupons, vouchers, stacking, usage holds for orders, legal limits as dated data
  • docs/TAX.md — taxes: the Vietnam tax data pack, computing taxes, tax profiles
  • docs/MONEY.md — money: the ledger, payments and flow modes, VietQR, accounting documents, exchange rates, printing, accounting exports, keeping records 10 years
  • docs/NOTIFICATIONS.md — notifications: kinds and categories, channels, consent and allowed hours for advertising, inbox and preferences, declaring a kind in a module
  • docs/MODULE_GUIDE.md — how to write a module, starting from the sample module modules/notes (not registered by default)

The first four documents steer the project and are written in Vietnamese, with technical terms kept in English. User-facing documentation (this README, the installation and usage guides, API descriptions) is written in English with a Vietnamese translation alongside.

Contributing

While you work, ./gate.sh --quick checks a change to one module in under a minute: it runs the tests of the crates you changed (and of the crates that depend on them) on SQLite only. Before a change is merged, run the full ./gate.sh; a change is accepted only when the full gate is green on both SQLite and PostgreSQL. Never commit secrets — only .env.example belongs in Git, never .env. CONTRIBUTING.md explains how to set up your machine, the rules that matter most and how to send a change.

Every commit carries a Signed-off-by line (DCO, git commit -s). Questions: SUPPORT.md. How decisions are made and how to propose a change: GOVERNANCE.md. Where the project is going: docs/ROADMAP.public.md. Building and listing your own module: docs/MODULE_ECOSYSTEM.md. Using the name: TRADEMARK.md.

Security

Found a vulnerability? Please do not open a public issue: report it privately as described in SECURITY.md, which also lists the versions that receive security fixes. docs/THREAT_MODEL.md describes the trust boundaries of the core, the controls at each one and what is still open.

  • MIT license (LICENSE-MIT)

at your option.

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in this project by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

Contributor Covenant 3.0 Code of Conduct

English · Tiếng Việt

Our Pledge

We pledge to make our community welcoming, safe, and equitable for all.

We are committed to fostering an environment that respects and promotes the dignity, rights, and contributions of all individuals, regardless of characteristics including race, ethnicity, caste, color, age, physical characteristics, neurodiversity, disability, sex or gender, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, language, philosophy or religion, national or social origin, socio-economic position, level of education, or other status. The same privileges of participation are extended to everyone who participates in good faith and in accordance with this Covenant.

Encouraged Behaviors

While acknowledging differences in social norms, we all strive to meet our community’s expectations for positive behavior. We also understand that our words and actions may be interpreted differently than we intend based on culture, background, or native language.

With these considerations in mind, we agree to behave mindfully toward each other and act in ways that center our shared values, including:

  1. Respecting the purpose of our community, our activities, and our ways of gathering.
  2. Engaging kindly and honestly with others.
  3. Respecting different viewpoints and experiences.
  4. Taking responsibility for our actions and contributions.
  5. Gracefully giving and accepting constructive feedback.
  6. Committing to repairing harm when it occurs.
  7. Behaving in other ways that promote and sustain the well-being of our community.

Restricted Behaviors

We agree to restrict the following behaviors in our community. Instances, threats, and promotion of these behaviors are violations of this Code of Conduct.

  1. Harassment. Violating explicitly expressed boundaries or engaging in unnecessary personal attention after any clear request to stop.
  2. Character attacks. Making insulting, demeaning, or pejorative comments directed at a community member or group of people.
  3. Stereotyping or discrimination. Characterizing anyone’s personality or behavior on the basis of immutable identities or traits.
  4. Sexualization. Behaving in a way that would generally be considered inappropriately intimate in the context or purpose of the community.
  5. Violating confidentiality. Sharing or acting on someone’s personal or private information without their permission.
  6. Endangerment. Causing, encouraging, or threatening violence or other harm toward any person or group.
  7. Behaving in other ways that threaten the well-being of our community.

Other Restrictions

  1. Misleading identity. Impersonating someone else for any reason, or pretending to be someone else to evade enforcement actions.
  2. Failing to credit sources. Not properly crediting the sources of content you contribute.
  3. Promotional materials. Sharing marketing or other commercial content in a way that is outside the norms of the community.
  4. Irresponsible communication. Failing to responsibly present content which includes, links or describes any other restricted behaviors.

Reporting an Issue

Tensions can occur between community members even when they are trying their best to collaborate. Not every conflict represents a code of conduct violation, and this Code of Conduct reinforces encouraged behaviors and norms that can help avoid conflicts and minimize harm.

When an incident does occur, it is important to report it promptly. To report a possible violation, email the Autoxide maintainers at thuongtamduy@live.com. Only the maintainers read this address. Say what happened, where (issue, pull request, discussion or elsewhere) and when, with links if you have them. You may write in English or Vietnamese. For security vulnerabilities, follow SECURITY.md instead.

Community Moderators take reports of violations seriously and will make every effort to respond in a timely manner. They will investigate all reports of code of conduct violations, reviewing messages, logs, and recordings, or interviewing witnesses and other participants. Community Moderators will keep investigation and enforcement actions as transparent as possible while prioritizing safety and confidentiality. In order to honor these values, enforcement actions are carried out in private with the involved parties, but communicating to the whole community may be part of a mutually agreed upon resolution.

Addressing and Repairing Harm

If an investigation by the Community Moderators finds that this Code of Conduct has been violated, the following enforcement ladder may be used to determine how best to repair harm, based on the incident’s impact on the individuals involved and the community as a whole. Depending on the severity of a violation, lower rungs on the ladder may be skipped.

  1. Warning
    1. Event: A violation involving a single incident or series of incidents.
    2. Consequence: A private, written warning from the Community Moderators.
    3. Repair: Examples of repair include a private written apology, acknowledgement of responsibility, and seeking clarification on expectations.
  2. Temporarily Limited Activities
    1. Event: A repeated incidence of a violation that previously resulted in a warning, or the first incidence of a more serious violation.
    2. Consequence: A private, written warning with a time-limited cooldown period designed to underscore the seriousness of the situation and give the community members involved time to process the incident. The cooldown period may be limited to particular communication channels or interactions with particular community members.
    3. Repair: Examples of repair may include making an apology, using the cooldown period to reflect on actions and impact, and being thoughtful about re-entering community spaces after the period is over.
  3. Temporary Suspension
    1. Event: A pattern of repeated violation which the Community Moderators have tried to address with warnings, or a single serious violation.
    2. Consequence: A private written warning with conditions for return from suspension. In general, temporary suspensions give the person being suspended time to reflect upon their behavior and possible corrective actions.
    3. Repair: Examples of repair include respecting the spirit of the suspension, meeting the specified conditions for return, and being thoughtful about how to reintegrate with the community when the suspension is lifted.
  4. Permanent Ban
    1. Event: A pattern of repeated code of conduct violations that other steps on the ladder have failed to resolve, or a violation so serious that the Community Moderators determine there is no way to keep the community safe with this person as a member.
    2. Consequence: Access to all community spaces, tools, and communication channels is removed. In general, permanent bans should be rarely used, should have strong reasoning behind them, and should only be resorted to if working through other remedies has failed to change the behavior.
    3. Repair: There is no possible repair in cases of this severity.

This enforcement ladder is intended as a guideline. It does not limit the ability of Community Managers to use their discretion and judgment, in keeping with the best interests of our community.

Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public or other spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official email address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

Attribution

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 3.0, permanently available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/3/0/.

Contributor Covenant is stewarded by the Organization for Ethical Source and licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0. To view a copy of this license, visit https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

For answers to common questions about Contributor Covenant, see the FAQ at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq. Translations are provided at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations. Additional enforcement and community guideline resources can be found at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/resources. The enforcement ladder was inspired by the work of Mozilla’s code of conduct team.

Contributing to Autoxide

English · Tiếng Việt

Thank you for helping. This guide is for people; if you work with an AI coding agent, point it at AGENTS.md (short, in English; the full internal rules are in CLAUDE.md), which holds the rules the agent follows. The rules below are the same, only shorter. Everyone taking part follows the code of conduct.

Before you start

  • Bugs: open an issue with the version, the database (SQLite or PostgreSQL) and the steps that reproduce it.
  • Security problems: do not open an issue; follow SECURITY.md.
  • New features: open an issue first and describe the problem you want to solve. The core stays neutral about business domains (no orders, stock or patients in the core — those belong in modules), and the order of work follows docs/ROADMAP.md, so a short discussion saves you from writing code that cannot be merged.

Set up your machine

You need:

  • Rust — rustup installs the exact toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml the first time you run cargo;
  • a C compiler (SQLite is compiled from source);
  • Docker, for the PostgreSQL and S3 tests of the full gate;
  • cargo-deny: cargo install cargo-deny --locked;
  • optionally gitleaks (the gate runs it in Docker otherwise).

On a fresh Linux x86_64 machine (for example a cloud agent session) run scripts/cloud-setup.sh instead of installing by hand: it installs the pinned toolchain and cargo-deny, gitleaks and cargo-nextest from prebuilt releases, checking pinned SHA-256 checksums. It is safe to run again.

Then:

git clone https://github.com/thuongtamduy/autoxide.git autoxide
cd autoxide
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
cargo test --workspace

The Git hooks check formatting and scan staged changes for secrets before each commit.

Check your change: two gates

The gate is the definition of “done”. There are two levels:

./gate.sh --quick

While you work, before each commit: formatting, lints, boundary checks, dependencies, secrets, and the tests of the crates you changed (and of the crates that depend on them), on SQLite only. It needs no Docker for the tests and usually takes a minute or two.

./gate.sh

Before you open a pull request: everything above, and every test on both SQLite and PostgreSQL (the gate starts throwaway Docker containers). A change is merged only when this gate is green.

When the gate is red, fix the code. Do not loosen the gate, turn off a lint or skip a test.

A change that only touches files listed in scripts/rust-free-paths.txt (documentation, the TypeScript SDK, changelog fragments, decisions) cannot change any Rust result: --quick skips Clippy for it, and on a pull request CI skips the Rust build and tests (the jobs still report success). Anything not in that list runs everything.

The rules that matter most

  • Both databases. Everything that touches the database — migrations, queries, transactions, indexes, tests — must work on SQLite and PostgreSQL. A feature that works on one only is not finished. Do not use types, functions or syntax only one of them has.
  • Module boundaries. Each module is its own crate under modules/ and owns its tables (named <module>_…). A module never reads, writes or joins another module’s tables and never has foreign keys to them; it calls other modules only through the traits they publish in pub mod api. cargo xtask check (part of the gate) enforces this.
  • Logic in services. HTTP handlers and MCP tools only take input, call a service and return the response; REST and MCP share the same service.
  • Errors have a stable code. Every error returned to clients is an autoxide_kernel::error::Error with a snake_case code (module errors start with <module>.) and a message that says what to fix. The code is a contract with clients: changing it is a breaking change. Each new code needs a Vietnamese translation in the crate’s locales/vi.json.
  • The API contract stays in sync. Every route is documented in OpenAPI. When you change the API or a setting, run cargo xtask regen: it regenerates every generated file in one go (docs/openapi.json, docs/mcp-tools.json, .env.example, the TypeScript SDK schema). The the gate on your machine checks them early (cargo xtask regen --check) and prints this command when one is stale (this step runs only locally; on CI the tests that keep the documents in sync with the code check them). Never change the behaviour of an existing /api/v1 endpoint in a breaking way; add a new one and deprecate the old.
  • Tests. New code comes with tests. Tests that touch the database use autoxide_testkit::TestDatabase, which gives each test an empty database on whichever of SQLite or PostgreSQL the gate is running.
  • No unsafe, no unwrap / expect / panic! outside tests. Return an error instead.
  • No secrets in Git. Only .env.example is committed, never .env.
  • Documentation in two languages. User-facing documents (README, guides in docs/, this file) have an English version and a Vietnamese one (*.vi.md) with the same content: change both in the same commit. Internal documents (CLAUDE.md, STACK.md, docs/ROADMAP.md, docs/DECISIONS.md) and code comments may be in Vietnamese.

The full list, with the reasons behind each rule, is in CLAUDE.md; past decisions are indexed by topic in docs/decisions/INDEX.md, which is generated and not committed: run cargo xtask decisions to create it.

Commits and pull requests

  • Keep a pull request to one change. Split unrelated changes.
  • For anything a user of Autoxide would notice, add a small file to changelog.d/ instead of editing CHANGELOG.md: name it <name>.<section>.md (added, changed, deprecated, removed, fixed or security) and write the English bullet points as they will appear in the changelog. They are folded into CHANGELOG.md at release time, so parallel pull requests never conflict there.
  • In the pull request, say what you changed, why, and confirm that ./gate.sh --quick is green (CI runs the rest, including PostgreSQL; the full ./gate.sh is required before a release).

Commit messages

Commit messages follow a light form of Conventional Commits:

<type>(<scope>): <short summary in the imperative mood, at most 72 characters>

<optional body: why the change is needed, what you considered, what it does not do>

Signed-off-by: Your Name <you@example.com>
  • type is one of feat, fix, docs, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore, revert. scope is optional: a module or crate name (orders, kernel).
  • Mark a breaking change with ! after the scope (feat(kernel)!: …) and explain it in the body. Breaking changes of the stable contract tier follow docs/COMPATIBILITY.md.
  • Write in English or Vietnamese. Explain why in the body when it is not obvious.
  • The pull request title is used as the squash-merge subject, so it follows the same form.

Sign your commits (DCO)

Autoxide uses the Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) instead of a contributor license agreement. By adding a Signed-off-by line you certify that you wrote the change or have the right to submit it under the project license. Add it with -s:

git commit -s -m "fix(notes): reject empty titles"

To sign commits you already made: git rebase --signoff origin/main and push again with --force-with-lease. The DCO sign-off job in CI fails when a commit of a pull request has no Signed-off-by line (when the branch the pull request targets has no .github/CODEOWNERS yet, which is true of old branches such as a release/X.Y cut from an old tag, nothing is checked; merge commits are not checked, so prefer rebasing over merging main into your branch). A pull request opened by a maintainer (a login listed in .github/CODEOWNERS on the branch the pull request targets, not in the pull request; GitHub authenticates the login) is exempt, including commits written by their agent sessions: maintainers are the licensors and answer for what they submit.

Contributions written with AI assistance

Autoxide is itself built with AI agents (CLAUDE.md), so AI-assisted contributions are welcome. The rules exist to keep a person accountable and the review load fair:

  • Say so. Tell us in the pull request description which tool helped and for what. Add a trailer such as Assisted-by: <tool or model> to the commit if the tool wrote a substantial part.
  • A person is responsible. The Signed-off-by line is yours, not the tool’s. You have read every line, you understand it and can explain it in review, and you ran ./gate.sh --quick yourself.
  • Check what the tool made up. Confirm every dependency, function and API exists in the pinned version (the repository’s check-library-api skill shows how). Remove invented references, and never paste secrets, personal data or customer data into a tool.
  • Do not send what you cannot defend. Unreviewed bulk output, many unrelated changes in one pull request, or replies to review comments that are pasted tool output may be closed without a detailed review.
  • Licensing. Do not submit output that you know copies code under an incompatible license.

Labels and where to start

Maintainers label issues so newcomers can find a first task: good first issue (small, well described, a maintainer will help), help wanted (we would like a contribution, any size) and the rest listed in GOVERNANCE.md. Comment on an issue before you start so two people do not do the same work.

License of your contribution

Autoxide is licensed under either of the Apache License, Version 2.0 or the MIT license, at the user’s option. Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution you intentionally submit for inclusion in Autoxide, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, is dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

Governance

English · Tiếng Việt

Autoxide is an open-source project run by a small group of maintainers. This document says who decides, how, and how you can change the project.

Roles

  • Users use Autoxide and report problems. No permission needed.
  • Contributors send pull requests, documentation, reviews or module ideas. See CONTRIBUTING.md.
  • Maintainers review and merge, cut releases, run the security process and keep the project on its roadmap. They are listed in .github/CODEOWNERS. The project owner (the first maintainer) holds the final say on direction and on the items marked “owner’s decision”.

A contributor becomes a maintainer after a sustained record of good changes and reviews, when an existing maintainer proposes it and no maintainer objects within seven days. A maintainer who is inactive for six months is moved to “emeritus” and can return by asking. The list of maintainers is the CODEOWNERS file; a maintainer is identified by GitHub login, which is also what exempts their pull requests from the DCO check.

How decisions are made

  1. Everyday changes (bug fixes, small features inside the current roadmap, documentation) need one maintainer’s approval and a green CI. The author does not approve their own change.
  2. Changes to the stable contract tier (public API of the kernel, testkit, a module’s api, REST/MCP contract, settings, migrations) or to security, money and tax code need an independent review from a second person and follow docs/COMPATIBILITY.md.
  3. Significant changes (new core capability, change of a convention, a library swap, anything that is expensive to undo) go through the RFC process below before code is written.
  4. Decisions are made by lazy consensus: a proposal stands when no maintainer objects within the review window (seven days for an RFC). If maintainers disagree and cannot settle it, the project owner decides and records the reason.
  5. The project’s long-lived decisions are written in docs/decisions/ (one file each) and are not reversed silently; a reversal is a new decision that names the one it replaces.

Proposing a change: the RFC process

An RFC (request for comments) is a short design document that you discuss before building.

  1. Discuss the idea first in an issue or a GitHub Discussion, to avoid writing an RFC for something already planned.
  2. Copy docs/rfcs/0000-template.md to docs/rfcs/NNNN-short-name.md (use the next free number) and fill it in. RFCs are written in English.
  3. Open a pull request titled rfc: <short name>. The pull request is the discussion.
  4. Maintainers and the community comment. The author updates the text. After the seven-day window with no unresolved objection, a maintainer merges it with status accepted, or closes it with status rejected and the reason.
  5. Accepted RFCs are implemented in later pull requests that link the RFC. An RFC that changes a lasting rule also adds a decision file in docs/decisions/.

See docs/rfcs/README.md for what needs an RFC and what does not.

Issue and pull request labels

LabelMeaning
good first issueSmall, well described, a maintainer will help; a good first contribution
help wantedWe want a contribution; any size, not necessarily easy
bugSomething does not work as documented
enhancementA new feature or improvement
documentationDocs only
questionA usage question (prefer GitHub Discussions)
needs-reproductionWe cannot reproduce it yet; the reporter is asked for steps
needs-rfcToo big for a pull request alone; write an RFC first
breaking-changeChanges the stable contract tier; needs a deprecation path
securityHandled privately first; see SECURITY.md
module, module:<name>Concerns a module (and which one)
db:sqlite, db:postgresOnly reproduces on one database
wontfix, duplicateClosed with a reason

A maintainer or the owner creates these labels once in the repository settings (the labels cannot be created by a file in the repository).

Code of conduct and conflicts

Everyone follows the code of conduct. Conduct reports go to the contact in that document, not to a public issue. Disagreements about technical direction follow the decision rules above.

Changing this document

Changes to this document are a pull request that needs approval from the project owner. Files that decide who is exempt from checks or how releases are made (.github/, scripts/) are listed in .github/CODEOWNERS; the repository settings must require a code owner review on main for that to bind (a setting of the project owner, see docs/OPENSSF.md).

Security policy

English · Tiếng Việt

Supported versions

Autoxide is a community project maintained by a small team. The periods below are what we aim for, not a service-level agreement: there is no paid support and no guaranteed response time.

From 1.0 (long-term support of each major version):

  • The latest minor release of the current major version (for example 1.5.x while 1.5 is the newest) gets every bug fix and security fix.
  • The previous minor release gets security fixes for 3 months after the next minor release comes out (for example 1.4.x until three months after 1.5.0), so you have time to upgrade.
  • When a new major version comes out, the last minor release of the previous major version gets security fixes for 6 months after the new major release.
  • Older releases are not patched.
VersionSecurity fixes
Latest 1.x minorYes
Previous 1.x minorFor 3 months after the next minor
Last minor of the previous major (after 2.0)For 6 months after the new major
Older releases (and 0.x once 1.0 is out)No

Before 1.0, while Autoxide is in its 0.x series, security fixes go into the latest minor release only; older 0.x releases are not patched.

Fixes ship as patch releases (1.5.2 → 1.5.3), which change nothing else, so they are safe to install right away (docs/COMPATIBILITY.md says what a patch release may contain). Update to the latest release of your line before reporting, and say in your report which version you tested. The CHANGELOG.md lists every release. How a fix reaches an older supported line (the backport process) is described in docs/COMPATIBILITY.md.

Security reviews

Before 1.0, the maintainers reviewed the whole code base for security problems in November 2026. It was an internal review carried out with AI assistance, not an audit by an independent third party. The scope, the method, every finding with its severity and fix, and the parts not yet covered are in docs/security/review-2026-11.md.

The threat model of the core — trust boundaries, the controls at each one, open items and suggested focus areas for outside testers — is in docs/THREAT_MODEL.md.

Reporting a vulnerability

Do not open a public issue, pull request or discussion for a security problem.

Report it privately through GitHub: open the repository’s Security tab and choose Report a vulnerability (GitHub’s private vulnerability reporting). Only the maintainers see the report, and it lets us work on a fix and an advisory with you before anything is public.

A useful report has:

  • the version (or commit) and the database (SQLite or PostgreSQL) you tested;
  • the configuration that matters, with secrets removed;
  • the steps or requests that reproduce the problem, and what an attacker gains;
  • whether you plan to publish, and when.

Please test only against your own installation. Do not access, change or delete data that is not yours, and do not run load tests against servers you do not operate.

What to expect

Autoxide is maintained by a small team, so these are targets, not guarantees:

StepTarget
We confirm we received the reportwithin 7 days
We tell you whether we accept it, and whywithin 14 days
A fixed release for an accepted reportas soon as possible, by severity
Public advisorywith the fixed release, at most 90 days after the report

We credit reporters in the advisory and the changelog unless you ask us not to. There is no bug bounty.

Disclosure policy

We follow coordinated disclosure:

  • We work on the fix in a private fork of the GitHub security advisory, and invite you to it if you want.
  • We ask GitHub to assign a CVE for accepted reports that affect a released version.
  • The advisory, the CVE and the fixed release are published together. The changelog entry for the fix is in the Security section of CHANGELOG.md.
  • If no fix is ready after 90 days, we publish the advisory anyway with the workarounds we know, unless we agree a later date with you (for example because the fix needs a change in a dependency).
  • If a vulnerability is already being exploited or is already public, we publish as soon as a fix or a workaround is ready, without waiting.
  • Please do not publish details before the advisory. If you think we are not responding, say so in the private report before going public.

Fixes for supported older lines (see the table above) are released at the same time when possible.

How we handle a report

The steps the maintainers follow, so that reporters know what happens and a second maintainer can take over:

  1. Receive. A report arrives as a private GitHub security advisory draft. One maintainer owns it and confirms receipt within 7 days (the table above). Nothing about it goes into a public issue, pull request, commit message or chat.
  2. Assess. Reproduce it on the latest release, on SQLite and on PostgreSQL where it can differ. Decide whether it is a vulnerability (see “What is not a vulnerability”), which versions are affected (check every supported line), and the severity as a CVSS v4.0 vector with a short reason. Tell the reporter the outcome within 14 days.
  3. Fix. Work in the temporary private fork of the advisory. Write the test that fails without the fix. A change to the kernel, security, money or tax code gets an independent review before it is merged, like any such change. Keep the fix small, and do not mention the problem in commit messages before the release.
  4. Release. Ship the fix as a patch release of the current line and of every supported older line (backporting). The changelog entry goes in the Security section. Critical and high severity: immediately and out of the normal schedule; medium and low: in the next patch release, or sooner.
  5. Publish. With the release, publish the advisory: affected and fixed versions, severity, a plain description of the impact, workarounds for people who cannot update at once, and credit to the reporter (unless they decline). Request the CVE from GitHub in the same advisory (“Request CVE ID”) for accepted reports that affect a released version.
  6. Learn. Search the code for the same mistake elsewhere, add a gate rule or a test that keeps it from coming back, and fix the runbook or the documentation if it misled someone. For exposure of personal data, the operators’ duties are in docs/DEPLOY.md.

Verifying a release

Releases are signed without long-lived keys (Sigstore, through GitHub Actions) and carry build provenance: docs/VERIFYING.md shows how to check the Docker image and the release files before you run them. A failed check is a security report.

What is not a vulnerability

These are known behaviours or outside the project, not security bugs:

  • Settings the documentation warns about: /metrics reachable from the internet after you turned on AUTOXIDE_HTTP_METRICS, AUTOXIDE_HTTP_CORS_ORIGINS=*, rate limiting turned off with 0, AUTOXIDE_HTTP_CLIENT_IP_HEADER set without a proxy in front, AUTOXIDE_SECRET_KEY or AUTOXIDE_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET left unset in production (the server logs a warning for each).
  • Volumetric denial of service: flooding a server with traffic. Report it if a single small request makes the server use far more memory, CPU or disk than it should.
  • Reports from automated scanners without a way to reproduce an actual impact, such as missing headers on JSON responses or version strings.
  • Vulnerabilities in a dependency that Autoxide cannot reach. cargo deny checks every release against the RustSec advisory database; if you found a path that does reach the vulnerable code, that is a report.
  • Problems in the user interface or other clients: they live in their own repositories. Autoxide only serves an API.
  • Anything that needs an administrator account to do what administrators may already do (for example, an administrator reading user data).

Getting help

English · Tiếng Việt

Autoxide is a community project. There is no paid support and no guaranteed response time; maintainers and other users help when they can.

Where to ask

You want to…Go to
Install, configure or use AutoxideRead README.md, docs/DEPLOY.md and docs/guides/, then ask in GitHub Discussions
Report a bugOpen an issue with the bug template
Suggest a featureOpen an issue with the feature template; larger changes use an RFC (GOVERNANCE.md)
Report a security problemNot in public: follow SECURITY.md
Report behaviour that breaks the code of conductFollow CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
ContributeCONTRIBUTING.md
Build a moduledocs/MODULE_GUIDE.md

Before you ask

  • Search the existing issues and discussions.
  • Run autoxide doctor and include its output: it checks the configuration and the database.
  • Say which version, which database (SQLite or PostgreSQL), and how you run Autoxide (binary, Docker, Kubernetes).
  • Never paste secrets, tokens or personal data. Remove them from logs first.

Supported versions

Which versions receive fixes is described in SECURITY.md; compatibility between versions in docs/COMPATIBILITY.md.

Using the Autoxide name

English · Tiếng Việt

The code of Autoxide is free: you may use, modify and redistribute it under the MIT or Apache-2.0 license, at your option (LICENSE-MIT, LICENSE-APACHE). Those licenses do not grant rights to the name and logo “Autoxide”. This page says how the name may be used so that people are never misled about what is official. It is a plain-language policy of the project, not legal advice, and the project does not claim a registered trademark.

You may, without asking

  • Say that your product, module or service works with, is built on or is compatible with Autoxide, and link to the project.
  • Name a module crate autoxide-<name> or <name>-for-autoxide and use the topic autoxide-module (docs/MODULE_ECOSYSTEM.md).
  • Write about Autoxide, teach it, review it, and use its name in articles, talks, videos, tutorials and job posts.
  • Make a fork and say it is a fork of Autoxide (“a fork of Autoxide”, with a link), as long as the fork has its own name.
  • Use the unmodified name in text to refer to the project, and the project’s logo (if one exists) unmodified to link to it.

You may not, without written permission

  • Name a product, company, domain, package or fork “Autoxide”, or something confusingly similar, as if it were the project (for example Autoxide Cloud offered as the project’s own service).
  • Say or suggest that your module, product or service is official, certified or endorsed by the Autoxide project when it is not. “Official module” means a module in the modules/ directory of this repository.
  • Use the name or logo in a way that implies the project’s maintainers are affiliated with you, sponsor you or stand behind your work.
  • Change the logo, or use it as the logo of your own product.

Modules and distributions

  • A community module may use the autoxide- prefix (see above) but must say in its README that it is not an official module unless it is listed in this repository.
  • A hosted service built on Autoxide may say “powered by Autoxide”. It must not be named in a way that makes users believe the Autoxide project operates it.
  • A modified distribution (binaries or images you build from changed code) must not be called “Autoxide” without saying it is modified and by whom.

Questions and requests

If you want to use the name in a way not covered here, or you see a use that misleads people, open an issue (or contact the maintainers as in SUPPORT.md). We would rather say yes to honest uses than have people guess.

Administrative units and addresses

Tiếng Việt

The address module keeps the official list of administrative units, shared by every tenant — for Vietnam since 2025-07-01: provinces and centrally governed cities (level 1) and communes, wards and special zones (level 2), without districts — and checks addresses for other modules (the public profile of a store, later the shipping addresses of customers).

Read it

No sign-in needed; answers carry an ETag that changes when a new list is imported and Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400.

RequestAnswer
GET /api/v1/address/provinces?country=VN&as_of=YYYY-MM-DDprovinces in force that day (default: today), in code order
GET /api/v1/address/provinces/{code}/communescommunes of a province
GET /api/v1/address/units?q=ha noi&province=01&level=2search by name, with or without accents
GET /api/v1/address/units/{code}one unit and the unit above it
POST /api/v1/address/validate{country, province_code, commune_code, line} → the address with names, or 422

MCP tools: address.list_provinces, address.list_communes, address.search_units, address.validate_address.

Import the list

The server ships with the Vietnamese list in force from 2025-07-01 (34 provinces and cities, 3,321 communes, wards and special zones, per decision QĐ 19/2025/QĐ-TTg; taken from provinces.open-api.vn v2, which republishes the statistics office’s list — check it against the original decision if you need legal certainty). Import it once per installation:

autoxide task address.import

autoxide doctor warns while nothing is imported, and when a newer list ships with an update.

To import another list (a later change by the state), get it from the official source — the decision QĐ 19/2025/QĐ-TTg (list and codes of administrative units, in force from 2025-07-01) and the electronic list of the statistics office (“Danh mục hành chính Việt Nam”) — never from an unofficial copy, and never generated. Put two files in a directory:

manifest.json:

{
  "country": "VN",
  "title": "QĐ 19/2025/QĐ-TTg",
  "source_url": "<address of the official file you downloaded>",
  "retrieved_on": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "effective_from": "2025-07-01"
}

units.csv (UTF-8, comma-separated, first line exactly as shown; codes keep their leading zeros):

level,code,name,kind,parent_code
1,01,<province name>,city,
2,00004,<commune name>,ward,01

kind is province, city, commune, ward or special_zone; a commune’s parent_code is the code of its province. Then:

autoxide task address.import path=/path/to/the/directory

Importing the same file again changes nothing. When the state changes the list, import the new one: units that disappeared or changed name, kind or province are closed on the new date and the new ones opened — addresses written before keep the names they were written with. autoxide doctor shows the list in use.

AI features

Tiếng Việt: AI.vi.md

Autoxide can use an AI model, chosen and paid for by you, to help editors and AI agents:

FeatureWhereNeeds
SEO check (no AI)GET /api/v1/content/entries/{id}/seo-checknothing
SEO suggestionsPOST /api/v1/content/entries/{id}/seo-suggestionstext model
Alt text suggestionsPOST /api/v1/media/{id}/alt-suggestionstext model that reads images
Translate a post or pagePOST /api/v1/content/entries/{id}/translatetext model
Search by meaningGET /api/v1/content/search, /public/searchembeddings
Limits for AI agentspermissions content.write_own, content.publish_ownnothing

Everything is off until you turn it on. No content leaves your server before you configure a provider. Suggestions never save anything: a person (or an agent) reviews them and saves with the usual PATCH. Translations are written as drafts and never published automatically.

Every endpoint and its error codes are in openapi.json (and at /api/docs when AUTOXIDE_HTTP_API_DOCS=true). The same features are MCP tools for AI agents: ai.status, content.seo_check, content.suggest_seo, content.translate, content.get_translation_request, content.search, media.suggest_alt.

Turning on text generation

Set a provider, a key and (for openai) a model, then check the settings:

autoxide ai check

It sends one tiny request and says in plain words whether it works (a few tokens).

Claude (Anthropic):

AUTOXIDE_AI_PROVIDER=anthropic
AUTOXIDE_AI_API_KEY=sk-ant-…            # your key
# AUTOXIDE_AI_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5     # the default

When Claude’s safety classifier declines a request, Anthropic reruns it on another model in the same call (AUTOXIDE_AI_ANTHROPIC_FALLBACK=true, the default). Set it to false for a model that does not support it, such as Claude Haiku.

OpenAI:

AUTOXIDE_AI_PROVIDER=openai
AUTOXIDE_AI_API_KEY=sk-…
AUTOXIDE_AI_MODEL=<an OpenAI model name>
# AUTOXIDE_AI_OPENAI_SEND_EFFORT=true   # only for reasoning models

Google Gemini (through its OpenAI-compatible endpoint):

AUTOXIDE_AI_PROVIDER=openai
AUTOXIDE_AI_BASE_URL=https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai
AUTOXIDE_AI_API_KEY=<your Gemini API key>
AUTOXIDE_AI_MODEL=<a Gemini model name>

Ollama, on your own server — nothing leaves the machine:

AUTOXIDE_AI_PROVIDER=openai
AUTOXIDE_AI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
AUTOXIDE_AI_MODEL=<a model you pulled>
AUTOXIDE_AI_IMAGES=false                # unless the model reads images
# AUTOXIDE_AI_OPENAI_SCHEMA_MODE=json_object   # if the server ignores JSON Schemas
# AUTOXIDE_AI_OPENAI_MAX_TOKENS_PARAM=max_tokens

vLLM, LM Studio and OpenRouter work the same way: openai plus their AUTOXIDE_AI_BASE_URL.

How answers are checked. Every request asks the model for JSON that follows a schema, and the server checks every answer again — some servers ignore the schema without saying so. A wrong answer is retried once, then reported (ai.output_invalid). Small local models fail this more often; use a capable model for translation.

Turning on embeddings (search by meaning)

Embeddings are separate from text generation: you may generate text with Claude and compute embeddings with Ollama.

AUTOXIDE_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=openai          # the /embeddings format
AUTOXIDE_EMBEDDING_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
AUTOXIDE_EMBEDDING_MODEL=bge-m3
AUTOXIDE_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS=1024

The same format is served by OpenAI (https://api.openai.com/v1; send AUTOXIDE_EMBEDDING_SEND_DIMENSIONS=true to shorten text-embedding-3-* vectors), Gemini and Voyage AI (Anthropic has no embeddings API and points to Voyage). Pick a multilingual model of about 1024 dimensions: bge-m3 and multilingual-e5-large handle Vietnamese well; models of 3072 dimensions use three times the memory.

Once on, every change of an entry updates its search index in the background, and an hourly job indexes what is missing — after you turn embeddings on or change the model or the dimensions (which rebuilds the whole index). Search keeps the vectors of a language in memory: about 41 MB per 10 000 passages at 1024 dimensions (a 1 500-word post is 5–6 passages); BENCHMARKS.md has the measured search times.

Search combines meaning and words (accents and case ignored): each result says how it matched (matched_by) and gives the best passage. With embeddings off, search matches words only. /api/v1/content/public/search (for anonymous readers) is off unless AUTOXIDE_CONTENT_PUBLIC_SEMANTIC_SEARCH=true; each public search costs an embeddings request, so searches by meaning have a budget per minute (AUTOXIDE_CONTENT_PUBLIC_SEARCH_PER_MINUTE, default 30, one budget shared by every reader and counted per server process) — past it, they match words only.

Costs and limits

  • Daily token limit: AUTOXIDE_AI_DAILY_TOKEN_LIMIT (default 2 000 000 tokens, text and embeddings together; 0 = no limit), counted in the database across all server processes. Past it, AI features answer 429 ai.quota_exceeded until midnight UTC. GET /api/v1/ai/status (permission ai.view) shows today’s use.
  • Metrics (with AUTOXIDE_HTTP_METRICS=true): ai_requests_total{purpose,outcome}, ai_tokens_total{purpose,direction}, ai_request_duration_seconds{purpose}.
  • Rough cost of translating a 1 500-word post (about 5 000 tokens in and 5 000 out), at Anthropic’s prices of 3 November 2026: Claude Opus 5.5 ≈ 0.12 USD, Claude Sonnet 5.5 ≈ 0.06 USD, Claude Haiku 5.5 ≈ 0.003 USD. An SEO suggestion costs a fraction of that. A local model costs nothing per request.

What is sent to the provider

FeatureSent
SEO suggestionstitle, summary, plain text of the draft (first 12 000 characters), names of the categories and tags of its language
Alt texta small copy of the image (at most 1280 px, never the original file), the language, the optional context you send
Translationthe text of the pinned revision in pieces — title, summary, SEO fields, image alt texts, paragraphs and headings with formatting as numbered tags; never links, image ids or code blocks
Searchthe text of each entry in passages (indexing), and each search query

Other modules send too: conversations sends the last messages of a conversation to draft a reply, orders sends product reviews to summarise them, support sends questions for suggested answers. These texts can hold personal data, and most providers process it outside Vietnam: that is a transfer of personal data abroad (Law 91/2025/QH15, Decree 356/2025/ND-CP — check with a legal professional). Name the provider as a recipient with its country in the purposes that use AI (/api/v1/compliance/purposes), keep an impact assessment for the transfer, or use a provider or a self-hosted model in Vietnam. The register does not list AI providers by itself yet (planned after 1.0).

Private images are sent only with AUTOXIDE_MEDIA_AI_SEND_PRIVATE=true. Logs never contain prompts, content, images or keys — only the task, the model, token counts and timing.

Translation in detail

POST /api/v1/content/entries/{id}/translate with {"locale": "vi"} answers 202 with a request; a background job does the work (each run is cut off after 4 minutes and retried; a request left running for 15 minutes is replaced by a new request for the same language):

  1. It pins the entry as it is now (a revision): later edits do not change this translation.
  2. The text is cut into pieces; formatting inside a paragraph becomes numbered tags (<m1>bold words</m1>, <br2/>) so word order can change between languages. The model never sees the JSON of the body, links or image ids.
  3. The answer is checked: every piece back exactly once, every tag exactly once, nothing empty. A bad answer is retried once, then the request fails with content.translation_invalid.
  4. The pieces are put back into the original structure (links and images come from the original) and saved as the draft of the translation: a new translation with a slug made from the translated title, or the existing translation — only if nobody changed it since the request; otherwise the request fails with content.translation_conflict and nothing is overwritten.

Follow it with GET /api/v1/content/translation-requests/{id} or webhooks (content.translation_succeeded, content.translation_failed). The translation is marked ai_generated; when the source changes afterwards, the admin API shows translation_outdated: true. Code blocks and embeds are not translated; names, numbers and addresses are kept.

AI agents: limits and review

Give each agent its own API key, with a short expiry and only what it needs:

The agent may…Permissions
write drafts, a person publishescontent.read, content.write_own
write and publish its own postscontent.read, content.write_own, content.publish_own
