API keys for programs and AI agents

Vietnamese: api-keys.vi.md. Examples use curl with API set to your server (export API=https://api.example.com), and the TypeScript SDK (sdk/typescript). They run as tests against every build, so they match the server of this version.

A program (a website build, a script, an AI agent) uses an API key instead of signing in. Give each key only the permissions it needs: it can never do more than you can, and a request beyond its permissions answers 403.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token
# save: REFRESH=.data.refresh_token

Create a key

Creating a key asks for your current password, so a stolen access token alone cannot mint a key that outlives it. Instead of the password you may send totp_code (a code from your authenticator app, when two-step sign-in is on) or a passkey (passkey_ceremony_id from POST /api/v1/auth/login/passkey/options and passkey_credential, the browser’s answer) — exactly one of the three. The key is shown once: store it now.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/api-keys" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"name":"Website build","permissions":["content.read"],"current_password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# expect: 201
# save: KEY=.data.key
# save: KEY_ID=.data.id

Use it

Send it like a token: Authorization: Bearer axk1_…. A key looks like axk1_<tenant ID, 32 hex digits>_<random part>: it names its tenant, so it works without the Autoxide-Tenant header or the tenant’s domain. Keys created by older versions start with axk_ and keep working.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/content/entries" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/content/entries" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  --json '{"kind":"post","title":"Not allowed"}'
# expect: 403

Requests with an API key have their own rate limit (AUTOXIDE_HTTP_RATE_LIMIT_API_KEY_PER_MINUTE, 120 by default). Past it the answer is 429 with Retry-After; see errors.

List and revoke

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/api-keys" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

curl -sS -X DELETE "$API/api/v1/auth/api-keys/$KEY_ID" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# expect: 204

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/content/entries" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"
# expect: 401

Every user’s keys (administrators)

With the permission auth.api_keys.manage, GET /api/v1/auth/all-api-keys (filter user_id=) lists the keys of every user with their owner’s name and email, never their secrets, and DELETE /api/v1/auth/all-api-keys/{id} revokes any of them — e.g. when a key leaks or its owner leaves. The audit log records who revoked it.

With the SDK

import { createClient } from "@autoxide/sdk";

// A build script. Never write the key in the code: read it from your secret store.
const api = createClient({ baseUrl: "https://api.example.com", token: "axk1_…" /* read it from your secret store */ });

for await (const entry of api.paginate("/api/v1/content/entries", { query: { status: "published" } })) {
  console.log(entry.title);
}

Signing in and staying signed in

Vietnamese: authentication.vi.md. Examples use curl with API set to your server (export API=https://api.example.com), and the TypeScript SDK (sdk/typescript). They run as tests against every build, so they match the server of this version.

Sign in

Send the email and password. The answer holds a short-lived access token (send it with every request) and a refresh token (to get the next pair). An account with two-step sign-in answers 202 with a challenge_id instead; finish with POST /api/v1/auth/login/mfa and the code.

On a server that hosts several tenants, sign in on the tenant’s domain or with the Autoxide-Tenant header. The tokens you get name their tenant, so the requests that follow — with the access token, /refresh, /logout, /login/mfa, and the links in password-reset and verification mails — need neither the header nor the domain. Sending a token together with a header (or domain) of another tenant is refused.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token
# save: REFRESH=.data.refresh_token

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/me" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Sign in with a link

When the server turns it on (AUTOXIDE_AUTH_LOGIN_LINK=true), POST /api/v1/auth/login/link with {"email": …} sends a one-time sign-in link (valid AUTOXIDE_AUTH_LOGIN_LINK_MINUTES, 15 by default). It always answers 202 the same way, whether or not the email has an account. Finish with POST /api/v1/auth/login/link/confirm and the token from the mail; the answer is the same as /login (tokens, or an mfa_token when two-step sign-in is on). Send "bind_device": true to get a device_secret and send it back with the token: the link then works only on this device.

Buyers: sign in with a phone number

Buyers can sign in, or create an account, with a code sent by SMS. It needs an SMS provider on the server; without one these endpoints answer 503 auth.phone_sign_in_unavailable.

  1. POST /api/v1/auth/phone/codes with {"phone": "0912345678"} answers 202 with a challenge_id. The answer is the same whether the number has an account or not.
  2. POST /api/v1/auth/phone/login with {"challenge_id": "…", "code": "123456", "name": "Lan"}. A number that already has a buyer account signs in to it (200). A new number creates a buyer account without email or password (201) when the shop lets buyers create accounts; name is used only then. Both answer with the same tokens as /login, or 202 when the account has two-step sign-in on.

Such an account has email set to "" until the buyer adds one. To confirm a sensitive change (POST /api/v1/auth/me/reauth) it uses "method": "phone_code" with a fresh phone_challenge_id and phone_code sent to its own number; after that it can add a passkey and sign in with it.

Limits against guessing codes (NIST SP 800-63B-4). A code lives at most 10 minutes (AUTOXIDE_COMPLIANCE_OTP_TTL_SECONDS, 60 to 600) and allows a few wrong tries. Per number:

  • codes per hour from one client (one IPv4 address, or one IPv6 /64) and from all clients together, and codes per day — sign-in codes and phone verification codes counted apart, so asking for sign-in codes never uses up the owner’s way to verify the number again (429 compliance.otp_throttled);
  • wrong codes per day (429 compliance.otp_daily_limit): for sign-in codes, from one client and from all clients together; for phone verification codes, only on the signed-in user’s own codes for the number (no “all clients” cap, so nobody else’s wrong codes block it);
  • wrong codes in a row, with no time window: from 90 the number is locked for clients that never signed in with it, and from 100 for every client (403 compliance.otp_locked).

A client that signed in with the number in the last 90 days does not count toward the “all clients” limits and keeps the last 10 tries of the 100, so strangers cannot lock the owner out of the networks they use. A right code resets the count. A locked number is unlocked when the owner signs in another way and verifies the number again in their account, or when the shop unlocks it — which also restarts the daily limit of wrong codes, while the limits on sending codes still apply (POST /api/v1/compliance/phone-locks/unlock, permission compliance.phone_locks.manage; MCP tool compliance.unlock_phone; autoxide task compliance.unlock_phone phone=…) — the way back in for an account that signs in only with its number. Remaining risk: mobile networks behind carrier NAT change address often; on a network the owner never signed in from, they can be locked out when strangers reach those limits. Offer buyers a second way to sign in (password or passkey) — NIST requires one for SMS codes.

Refresh before the access token expires

expires_in says how many seconds the access token lives. Shortly before, exchange the refresh token for a new pair. Each refresh token works once: keep the new one.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/refresh" --json '{"refresh_token":"'"$REFRESH"'"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token
# save: NEW_REFRESH=.data.refresh_token

Sending an old refresh token again looks like a stolen token: the server refuses it (auth.refresh_token_reused) and ends the whole session, so the newest refresh token stops working too. Sign in again.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/refresh" --json '{"refresh_token":"'"$REFRESH"'"}'
# expect: 401

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/refresh" --json '{"refresh_token":"'"$NEW_REFRESH"'"}'
# expect: 401

Sign out

Ending a session takes its refresh token. Its access tokens stop working at once (code auth.session_ended), without waiting for them to expire; the same happens when you end a session from the list below, change your password, or an administrator signs you out or disables the account.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token
# save: REFRESH=.data.refresh_token

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/logout" --json '{"refresh_token":"'"$REFRESH"'"}'
# expect: 204

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/me" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# expect: 401

Your sessions

GET /api/v1/auth/me/sessions lists the devices signed in to your account: user_agent, sign_in_method (password, password_and_mfa, passkey, email_link, password_change) and, when the server’s reverse proxy tells it (AUTOXIDE_AUTH_COUNTRY_HEADER, e.g. CF-IPCountry), the approximate country. The IP address is never kept. End a session you do not know with DELETE /api/v1/auth/me/sessions/{id}.

Your account

PATCH /api/v1/auth/me changes your display name (name), preferred language (locale: en or vi) and time zone (time_zone, IANA, e.g. Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh); null clears the language or time zone. Mails sent later (password reset, email change notice) use your preferred language.

Sensitive changes — creating an API key, changing your email, turning on two-step sign-in, adding a passkey, deleting your account — need proof that it is you. Send your current_password, or first get a short-lived confirmation token with POST /api/v1/auth/me/reauth ({"method": "password" | "totp" | "passkey" | "email_link", …}) and send it as reauth_token. Each token works once, for AUTOXIDE_AUTH_REAUTH_MINUTES (10 by default). Accounts without a password use passkey, totp or email_link.

A role can require two-step sign-in (requires_mfa, also on the built-in admin role). Until the account turns on an authenticator app or adds a passkey, that role’s permissions are left out and GET /api/v1/auth/me answers mfa_required: true.

With the SDK

Give the client a function for the token, so each request reads the current one:

import { createClient } from "@autoxide/sdk";

let tokens = { access: "", refresh: "" };
const api = createClient({ baseUrl: "https://api.example.com", token: () => tokens.access });

const signedIn = await api.post("/api/v1/auth/login", {
  body: { email: "admin@example.com", password: "correct horse battery staple" },
});
if ("access_token" in signedIn) {
  tokens = { access: signedIn.access_token, refresh: signedIn.refresh_token };
}

const me = await api.get("/api/v1/auth/me");
console.log(me.email, me.permissions);

const next = await api.post("/api/v1/auth/refresh", { body: { refresh_token: tokens.refresh } });
tokens = { access: next.access_token, refresh: next.refresh_token };

Automating work with rules

Vietnamese: automations.vi.md. Examples use curl with API set to your server (export API=https://api.example.com). They run as tests against every build, so they match the server of this version.

An automation rule says “when something happens and the conditions hold, then run these actions”, without writing code. Each action is an MCP tool that the server already has, so a rule can do exactly what you could do yourself through the REST API or MCP with the same permissions — nothing more.

  • Trigger: an event of a module ({"type": "event", "event": "<module>.<event>"}), a schedule ({"type": "schedule", "every": "hour" | "day" | "week", "weekday": "monday", "hour": 9, "minute": 0}), a manual call ({"type": "manual"}), or a figure leaving its usual range ({"type": "metric", …}, below).
  • Conditions: a tree of all / any / not over comparisons {"field": "event.total", "op": "gt", "value": 5000000}. Operators: eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte, in, contains, exists. No free-form expressions: a rule is checked when you save it and behaves the same everywhere.
  • Actions, in order: {"tool": "<module>.<tool>", "arguments": {…}}, {"wait": {"minutes": 60}} (up to 30 days), {"stop_if": <condition>}, {"notify": {"title": "…", "body": "…"}} (a notification to the rule’s owner). Values may use templates: "{{ event.code }}" alone keeps the type of the value; text such as "Order {{ event.code }}" is filled as text. Templates see event (the trigger’s data), trigger (what started the run) and steps (results of earlier steps: steps.0.result).

GET /api/v1/automations/catalog lists the events, metrics and tools you may use, with each tool’s input schema.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/automations/catalog" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Create a rule

Saving checks everything at once and reports every problem in errors: unknown events or tools (automations.trigger_unknown, automations.tool_unknown), tools you lack the permission for (automations.permission_missing), and arguments that do not fit a tool’s input schema. A rule runs with the current permissions of the person it runs as (run_as: the author, or whoever last changed its actions or enabled it); if that person loses a permission the rule needs, the rule pauses itself. A rule also never uses a permission its run_as did not have when they saved or enabled it (the limit is by permission name; the scope is the person’s current one). Rules saved before this limit existed get it the next time someone edits or enables them.

When every way into the run_as account is cut, the account’s rules pause with status_reason owner_access_revoked. This happens when the account is locked out (for example its owner reported a sign-in that was not them), recovered by email, disabled or deleted — and also when its owner changes their password and signs out everywhere. Unlocking the account does not turn the rules back on: someone with the permissions checks each rule and enables it again (and becomes its run_as).

Runs follow the rule they belong to. Whenever a rule stops being active (paused for any reason, disabled, deleted), its runs still waiting (a wait step, an approval) end with automations.rule_not_active instead of continuing. A run that started before the rule was edited (even only renamed) or enabled again stops with automations.rule_changed: it never finishes old actions under a new definition or a new person responsible.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/automations/rules" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"name":"Big orders","trigger":{"type":"manual"},"conditions":{"field":"event.total","op":"gte","value":5000000},"actions":[{"notify":{"title":"Big order {{ event.code }}","body":"Total: {{ event.total }}"}}]}'
# expect: 201
# save: RULE=.data.id

Rules made by an AI agent (an API key of kind agent) wait in pending_approval until a person enables them with POST /api/v1/automations/rules/{id}/enable; the rule then runs as that person.

Try it without doing anything

A dry run evaluates the conditions on a sample, fills the templates and checks tools and permissions — it calls no tool.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/automations/rules/$RULE/test" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"event_sample":{"total":6000000,"code":"DH1"}}'

Run it and read the log

Runs happen in the background. Each run keeps a log of every step: status, result, error code, and the step’s Idempotency-Key (automation:<run id>:<step>) — retrying a failed run (POST /runs/{id}/retry) starts at the failed step and never does a finished step twice.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/automations/rules/$RULE/run" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"input":{"total":6000000,"code":"DH1"}}'
# expect: 202
# save: RUN=.data.id

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/automations/runs/$RUN" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/automations/runs?rule_id=$RULE" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Risky steps wait for a person

A step whose tool deletes or overwrites data (or needs approval when an agent calls it) stops the run in awaiting_approval each time. A person with automations.run and the tool’s own permission approves (POST /runs/{id}/approve) or rejects (POST /runs/{id}/reject) it; the work inbox lists such runs (automations.approvals).

Loops and limits

Events caused by a rule’s actions never start the same rule again, and a chain of rules (A’s action starts B, …) stops after 3 rules: the run is logged as skipped with automations.loop_detected. A rule that starts more than AUTOXIDE_AUTOMATIONS_MAX_RUNS_PER_HOUR runs in an hour (default 1000) pauses itself (status_reason: rate_limit).

Alerts when a figure is unusual

A metric trigger checks a figure once a day at hour:minute (the rule’s time zone) and compares it with a fixed threshold (below, above) or with its usual level — the average of the same weekday over the 4 previous weeks (drop_pct, rise_pct, a percentage):

{"type": "metric", "metric": "fact:<kind>", "currency": "VND", "operator": "drop_pct", "value": 30, "hour": 8}
  • fact:<kind>: the daily total of a report figure that a module declares (the previous whole day in local time).
  • summary:<id>: a dashboard figure, read at check time with the rule owner’s permissions; ratios in basis points (1% = 100).

The statistics are simple and deterministic, and the run’s event.explanation says why, e.g. “… was 12000000, 45% lower than the average of the 4 previous Mondays: 21800000”. Without four weeks of data the rule does not alert, and it alerts at most once per day. Ready-made templates (from the modules that own the figures) are at GET /api/v1/automations/templates.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/automations/templates" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Uploading large files straight to storage

Vietnamese: direct-uploads.vi.md. Examples use curl with API set to your server (export API=https://api.example.com), and the TypeScript SDK (sdk/typescript). They run as tests against every build, so they match the server of this version.

When files are stored on S3 (or an S3-compatible service), a large file does not have to pass through the API server: you ask for a signed upload link, send the file straight to the storage, then ask the server to complete the upload. The server reads the file back and checks it before creating the record. It works for plain files (/api/v1/files/uploads) and for the media library (/api/v1/media/uploads, which also checks the real type of the content, as an upload through the server does).

When files are stored on the server’s disk there is no link: the server answers 409 (files.direct_upload_unavailable) and you upload through POST /api/v1/files (or POST /api/v1/media) as usual.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token

1. Ask for a link

Give the file’s name, media type, exact size in bytes and SHA-256 (64 hex digits, e.g. sha256sum file). Every problem with them is reported at once (422). This example server stores files on disk, so it answers 409; on S3 it answers 201 with the link.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/files/uploads" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"name":"hello.txt","content_type":"text/plain","size":5,"sha256":"2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824"}'
# expect: 409

On S3 the answer looks like this (Location is the file the upload will become):

{"data": {"id": "0193f2a0-…", "method": "PUT", "url": "https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/files/0193f2a0-…?X-Amz-Signature=…",
  "headers": {"content-length": "5", "content-type": "text/plain", "x-amz-checksum-sha256": "LPJNul+wow4m6DsqxbninhsWHlwfp0JecwQzYpOLmCQ="},
  "expires_at": "2026-11-18T10:15:00Z"}}

2. Send the file to the link

Send the content with exactly the given method and headers before expires_at (15 minutes by default, AUTOXIDE_FILES_DIRECT_UPLOAD_SECONDS). The signature covers the type and the checksum: Amazon S3 refuses another file. The request goes to the storage, not to the API server.

curl -sS -X PUT "$URL" -H 'content-type: text/plain' \
  -H 'x-amz-checksum-sha256: LPJNul+wow4m6DsqxbninhsWHlwfp0JecwQzYpOLmCQ=' --data-binary @hello.txt

3. Complete the upload

curl -sS -X POST "$API/api/v1/files/uploads/$ID/complete" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
  • 201 with the new file (the same shape as POST /api/v1/files); calling it again answers 200 with the same file, so retrying is safe.
  • 409 files.upload_incomplete: the storage does not have the file yet — send it, then call again.
  • 422 files.upload_mismatch: the file’s size or SHA-256 differs from what you declared. It was removed; send the right file to the same link and complete again before the link expires.
  • 409 files.upload_expired: start a new upload.

Uploads that are never completed are removed by a job an hour after they expire. Plain files reserve their declared size in the tenant’s storage quota from step 1 until they are completed or removed.

Media library

POST /api/v1/media/uploads takes the same fields plus folder_id, tags and org_id, and POST /api/v1/media/uploads/{id}/complete creates the item. Completing reads the whole item back and checks it like an upload through the server: the content must really be of the declared type (415 media.content_mismatch), an SVG must not contain active content, images get their width and height. Media items up to AUTOXIDE_MEDIA_DIRECT_MAX_BYTES (1 GiB by default) can be uploaded this way; for large items raise AUTOXIDE_HTTP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS so the check fits in one request.

For AI agents (MCP)

The tools files.create_upload / files.confirm_upload and media.create_upload / media.confirm_upload do the same; the agent sends the file to the link itself.

Set up the bucket

A browser can only send the file if the bucket allows it (CORS): allow PUT from your website’s origin with the headers content-type and x-amz-checksum-sha256 — see “Uploads straight to S3” in docs/DEPLOY.md.

With the SDK

import { createClient } from "@autoxide/sdk";

const api = createClient({ baseUrl: "https://api.example.com", token: "axk1_…" /* read it from your secret store */ });
declare const file: File; // e.g. from <input type="file">

const bytes = new Uint8Array(await file.arrayBuffer());
const digest = await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", bytes);
const sha256 = [...new Uint8Array(digest)].map((b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")).join("");

const link = await api.post("/api/v1/files/uploads", {
  body: { name: file.name, content_type: file.type, size: file.size, sha256 },
});
const headers = { ...link.headers };
delete headers["content-length"]; // the browser sets it
await fetch(link.url, { method: link.method, headers, body: bytes });
const saved = await api.post("/api/v1/files/uploads/{id}/complete", { path: { id: link.id } });

Reading errors

Vietnamese: errors.vi.md. Examples use curl with API set to your server (export API=https://api.example.com), and the TypeScript SDK (sdk/typescript). They run as tests against every build, so they match the server of this version.

Every error is RFC 9457 Problem Details (application/problem+json):

  • code — stable, for programs: branch on it, never on the text. A module’s codes start with its name (content.not_found).
  • detail — a sentence for people, in the language of Accept-Language (en by default, or vi).
  • errors — on 422, one entry per invalid input field: field (e.g. items[0].url), code, detail. Every problem of the request is listed at once.
  • the X-Request-Id header — quote it when you report a problem.
  • Retry-After (header) — on 429 (too many requests) and 503 (the server is restarting), the seconds to wait.
curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token
# save: REFRESH=.data.refresh_token

Not signed in:

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/content/entries"
# expect: 401

Invalid input, with the details in Vietnamese:

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/content/entries" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Accept-Language: vi' \
  --json '{"kind":"essay","title":"x"}'
# expect: 422

A misspelt or unknown field in the body is refused with 422 (code invalid_body, the detail names the field and the fields expected) rather than silently ignored:

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","pasword":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# expect: 422

A record that does not exist:

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/content/entries/0193e3a4-7b1c-7f00-9a51-6f2b8c0d4e11" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# expect: 404

Changing a record: If-Match, 428 and 412

Reading one record returns its version in the ETag header. Endpoints that change a record take it back in If-Match, so two people never overwrite each other. Endpoints whose description says If-Match is required answer 428 (code precondition_required) without it; a version that is no longer current gets 412 (code precondition_failed): read the record again, apply your change to what you read, and send the new ETag.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/content/entries" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"kind":"post","title":"First title"}'
# expect: 201
# save: ENTRY=.data.id

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/content/entries/$ENTRY" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# save: ENTRY_ETAG=header:etag

curl -sS -X PATCH "$API/api/v1/content/entries/$ENTRY" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"title":"Second title"}'
# expect: 428

curl -sS -X PATCH "$API/api/v1/content/entries/$ENTRY" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "If-Match: $ENTRY_ETAG" --json '{"title":"Second title"}'
# expect: 200

curl -sS -X PATCH "$API/api/v1/content/entries/$ENTRY" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "If-Match: $ENTRY_ETAG" --json '{"title":"Third title"}'
# expect: 412

With the SDK

Errors throw an AutoxideError:

import { AutoxideError, createClient } from "@autoxide/sdk";

const api = createClient({ baseUrl: "https://api.example.com", token: "axk1_…" /* read it from your secret store */, language: "vi" });

try {
  await api.post("/api/v1/content/entries", { body: { kind: "post", title: "" } });
} catch (error) {
  if (!(error instanceof AutoxideError)) throw error;
  switch (error.code) {
    case "validation_failed":
      for (const field of error.errors) console.log(field.field, field.detail);
      break;
    case "rate_limited":
      console.log(`try again in ${error.retryAfter} s`);
      break;
    default:
      console.log(error.status, error.detail, error.requestId);
  }
}

Upgrading clients: every list is a page

Vietnamese: list-pages-upgrade.vi.md. For reading lists in general, see Reading long lists.

Before version 1.0, every GET endpoint that returns a list was changed in place to return one page. The path did not change; the shape of the answer did. A client written for the old shape reads only the first 50 items and must be updated.

What changed

Before, some lists answered the whole list in data:

{"data": [{"id": "…"}, {"id": "…"}]}

Now every list answers one page, with pagination next to data:

{"data": [{"id": "…"}, {"id": "…"}], "pagination": {"limit": 50, "next_cursor": "…"}}
  • data holds the items of this page, as before.
  • pagination.limit is the page size that was applied.
  • pagination.next_cursor is where the next page starts; null (or absent) means this is the last page.
  • pagination.total is the number of items matching your filters, over all pages. It is only there on the first page of a request sent with count=true.

The same holds for the MCP tools that list things: they take the same parameters and answer the same {"data": […], "pagination": {…}}.

How to read a whole list

Every list takes the same four query parameters:

ParameterMeaning
limitItems per page, 1 to 200. Defaults to 50.
cursorThe next_cursor of the previous page. Leave it out for the first page.
orderasc or desc. The default depends on the list (see below).
counttrue to also get pagination.total on the first page. Counting costs a query: ask only when you show it.

Ask for the first page, then, while next_cursor is not null, ask again with cursor set to it and the same filters, order and sort. A cursor from another list, or from the same list with another sort, answers 422 with the problem on cursor. The cursor stays valid while you read, even when items are added.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/content/entries?limit=100&count=true" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/content/entries?limit=100&cursor=$CURSOR" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Stop when next_cursor is null, not when a page is shorter than limit. Lists that check your permission on each item (for example GET /api/v1/kernel/custom-fields without target, or the approval requests) read a bounded number of rows per request: a page may hold fewer items than limit, even none, and still have a next_cursor. Their description in the API reference says so.

Which order a list uses

Each list says in its description what it is ordered by. There are three kinds:

  • Newest first — lists with no order other than when items were created (orders, refunds, events, notes…): order defaults to desc; order=asc gives the oldest first.
  • Natural order — lists with a meaningful order of their own (position, name, code, depth in a tree…): order defaults to asc (first position, A to Z); order=desc reverses it.
  • Follows sort — lists with a sort parameter: the default order follows the chosen column — desc (newest first) for times such as created_at and updated_at, asc for names, codes, positions and sizes. The description of sort lists the default of each value. Sending order yourself always wins.

The order is stable from page to page: items are never repeated or skipped while you follow next_cursor.

With the TypeScript SDK

paginate() follows next_cursor for you and yields the items one by one:

import { createClient } from "@autoxide/sdk";

const api = createClient({ baseUrl: "https://api.example.com", token: "axk1_…" /* read it from your secret store */ });

// Every record that uses an image, whatever the number of pages.
for await (const usage of api.paginate("/api/v1/kernel/records/{kind}/{id}/usages", {
  path: { kind: "media.item", id: "0190a4c2-0000-7000-8000-000000000001" },
  query: { limit: 100 },
})) {
  console.log(usage.kind, usage.id, usage.title);
}

To show one page at a time (a table with a “next” button) and a total, call get(); a list keeps its pagination:

import { createClient } from "@autoxide/sdk";

const api = createClient({ baseUrl: "https://api.example.com", token: "axk1_…" /* read it from your secret store */ });

const first = await api.get("/api/v1/content/entries", { query: { limit: 20, count: true } });
console.log(`${first.pagination.total ?? "?"} entries`);
let cursor = first.pagination.next_cursor;
while (cursor) {
  const page = await api.get("/api/v1/content/entries", { query: { limit: 20, cursor } });
  for (const entry of page.data) console.log(entry.id, entry.title);
  cursor = page.pagination.next_cursor;
}

With MCP tools

A tool that lists things takes limit, cursor, order and count (plus sort when the REST endpoint has it) with the same meaning, and answers {"data": […], "pagination": {…}}. An agent calls the tool again with cursor set to pagination.next_cursor and the same other arguments until it is null. See Connecting an AI agent over MCP.

Exceptions

Three lookups answer a list in data without pagination, because they return at most one item per key you send (at most 100 keys), in the order you sent them: GET /api/v1/catalog/variants?code=…, GET /api/v1/comments/public/counts and GET /api/v1/inventory/public/availability.

What changed, endpoint by endpoint

The changelog lists every endpoint and tool that changed, with its default order and the behaviour changes (lists whose order changed, limit parameters of a single endpoint replaced by the shared one): see the “Changed” section of CHANGELOG.md for this release, entries marked Breaking (pre-1.0, D-20261125-list-pages).

Connecting MCP clients with OAuth sign-in

Vietnamese: mcp-oauth.vi.md.

With OAuth sign-in on, a person adds your server to Claude, ChatGPT, an IDE or any MCP client by its address alone. The client opens a browser, the person signs in to your interface and picks what the client may do, and the client receives tokens that never carry more than that. Nobody copies or pastes a key. Without OAuth, clients still connect with an API key (Connecting an AI agent over MCP).

Autoxide follows the MCP authorization specification (2026-07-28): OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414), resource indicators (RFC 8707), client metadata documents and, for older clients, dynamic client registration (RFC 7591).

1. Turn it on

OAuth sign-in is on when both of these are set:

SettingValue
AUTOXIDE_HTTP_PUBLIC_URLThe address clients reach your server at, without a path, e.g. https://api.example.com. It is the OAuth issuer. With a path (https://example.com/api) OAuth stays off and the log says why.
AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OAUTH_CONSENT_URLThe page of your interface where a signed-in person approves a client, with {token} where the request token goes, e.g. https://app.example.com/connect?request={token}.

Optional:

SettingDefaultMeaning
AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OAUTH_DYNAMIC_REGISTRATIONtrueLet clients register themselves at POST /api/v1/auth/oauth/register. MCP 2026-07-28 deprecates this in favour of client metadata documents; keep it on while the clients you care about still use it.
AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OAUTH_GRANT_DAYS90How long an approval lasts at most (1–365 days). The person approving can choose less. Afterwards the client asks again.
AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OAUTH_ALLOW_PRIVATE_NETWORKSfalseFetch client metadata documents from private addresses and over http://. Tests only: anyone can name a client, so in production this would let them make your server call your internal network.

Check with autoxide doctor (the mcp_oauth line names the issuer, or says why OAuth is off), then:

curl -sS https://api.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp
curl -sS https://api.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server

The first names the resource (https://api.example.com/mcp) and its authorization server; the second lists the endpoints (/api/v1/auth/oauth/authorize, /token, /revoke, /register). While OAuth is off both answer 404 with code oauth_unavailable.

Clients that run in someone else’s cloud (Claude and ChatGPT on the web) reach your server from the internet: AUTOXIDE_HTTP_PUBLIC_URL must be an https:// address they can open. A client on the same machine (an IDE, Claude Code) can use a local address.

2. What happens when a client connects

  1. The client calls /mcp without a token and gets 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="…/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp". From there it finds the authorization server.
  2. The client identifies itself: by a client metadata document (its client_id is an https:// URL of a JSON document the server fetches), or by registering at /register.
  3. The client opens the browser at /api/v1/auth/oauth/authorize with PKCE (S256). The server checks every parameter and sends the browser to your consent page with a request token. Any parameter error answers 400 right there and never redirects back to the client.
  4. On the consent page the person signs in (if needed), sees who is asking and chooses permissions. The page approves or denies through the API, and the browser goes back to the client with a code.
  5. The client exchanges the code at /token and calls /mcp with Authorization: Bearer axo1_….

Tokens:

  • The access token (axo1_…) is short-lived; the refresh token (axr1_…) gives a new pair once and is then used up. Clients must refresh one at a time: sending an old refresh token again (or two refreshes at once) is treated as theft and revokes the approval.
  • A client for /mcp may also use /mcp/<module>. REST at /api/v1 is a separate resource the client must ask for (resource=https://api.example.com/api/v1).
  • The client acts as the person, with kind agent, never with more than the approved permissions and what the person can do right now. If the person loses a permission, the client loses it too.
  • tools/list shows only the tools the approval allows. Calling something the person could do but did not approve answers 403 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="…", so the client can ask for more.

Only staff accounts approve clients (customers of a shop cannot). The approval belongs to the tenant the person was signed in to on the consent page.

3. The consent page of your interface

Autoxide has no web pages of its own: the consent page lives in your interface, at the address in AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OAUTH_CONSENT_URL. It needs a signed-in session of the person (password, passkey, single sign-on…). An API key or an OAuth token cannot read or decide requests (403 auth.session_required), so a client can never approve itself.

  1. Keep the request token. Read request from the address. If the person is not signed in, sign them in first and come back with the token. Requests wait 10 minutes.

  2. Show the request: GET /api/v1/auth/oauth/requests/{token}.

    {
  "data": {
    "client_id": "https://client.example.com/oauth/metadata.json",
    "client_host": "client.example.com",
    "client_name": "Example assistant",
    "registration": "cimd",
    "redirect_uri": "https://client.example.com/oauth/callback",
    "redirect_host": "client.example.com",
    "localhost_redirect": false,
    "resource": "https://api.example.com/mcp",
    "requested_scope": ["content.*"],
    "permissions": [
      {"name": "content.read", "description": "…", "risk": "read", "requested": true},
      {"name": "content.write_own", "description": "…", "risk": "write", "requested": true}
    ],
    "current_permissions": null,
    "expires_at": "2026-11-27T10:10:00Z"
  }
}
    • Show client_host and redirect_host prominently. client_name is chosen by the client and not verified: show it next to the host, never alone.
    • registration is cimd (metadata document: the host really published it) or dynamic (self-registered: anyone could have chosen that name).
    • When localhost_redirect is true, warn: the code goes back to a program on this device, and any program there could pretend to be this client.
    • permissions are the ones the person holds, narrowed to what the client asked for. Pre-select those with requested: true; let the person untick any. A prefix such as content.* is only a request: the approval stores the exact names chosen, so permissions added to the server later never slip into an old approval.
    • current_permissions is the person’s existing approval of this client for this resource, if any.

  3. Approve: POST /api/v1/auth/oauth/requests/{token}/approve with

    {"permissions": ["content.read", "content.write_own"], "days": 30}

    days is optional (default and maximum: AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OAUTH_GRANT_DAYS). A permission whose risk is destructive, sensitive_data or money also needs "reauth_token" from POST /api/v1/auth/me/reauth (the person confirms with their password, a passkey or a code); without it the answer is 422 and the request keeps waiting.

  4. Or deny: POST /api/v1/auth/oauth/requests/{token}/deny.

  5. Send the browser on: both answer {"data": {"redirect_to": "…"}}. Set window.location to it: the client receives the code (or error=access_denied) with its state and the issuer iss.

4. Connecting clients

The address to give every client is https://api.example.com/mcp (or /mcp/<module> for one module’s tools only). Menu names change between versions; the client’s own documentation is the reference.

  • Claude (claude.ai, the desktop and mobile apps): add a custom connector with the server address. Claude opens your consent page in the browser; after approving, the tools appear in chats where the connector is enabled. Claude connects from the internet, so the address must be public https://.
  • Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http autoxide https://api.example.com/mcp, then run /mcp in a session and choose to authenticate; the browser opens on this machine.
  • ChatGPT: in the settings for connectors / apps (developer mode where required), create a connector with the server address and OAuth authentication. ChatGPT also connects from the internet.
  • Other clients (IDEs, agent frameworks, the MCP SDKs): any client that implements MCP authorization works the same way: give it the address and let it open the browser. Clients that keep the redirect on the device use http://127.0.0.1:<any port>/…; the server accepts any port for 127.0.0.1 and [::1], but not for the name localhost (RFC 8252).

A client that cannot do OAuth still connects with an API key in the Authorization header (Connecting an AI agent over MCP).

5. Seeing and revoking approvals

  • The person: GET /api/v1/auth/me/oauth-grants lists their approvals (newest first, including revoked and expired); DELETE /api/v1/auth/me/oauth-grants/{id} revokes one. Tokens stop working at the next request.
  • Administrators with auth.oauth_grants.manage: GET /api/v1/auth/oauth-grants and DELETE /api/v1/auth/oauth-grants/{id} for everyone in the tenant. Revoking (both endpoints) needs the person’s own signed-in session, working directly in their own tenant: an API key or an OAuth token gets 403 auth.session_required.
  • The client itself: POST /api/v1/auth/oauth/revoke (RFC 7009) with the access or refresh token revokes the whole approval.
  • Automatically: locking, disabling or deleting the account, account recovery, a password change that signs out other sessions, and “sign out everywhere” revoke every approval of the person. Automation rules created through a client pause when its approval is revoked.

Every approval and revocation is an event in the audit log (auth.oauth_granted, auth.oauth_revoked), and every change made through a client records which client acted for whom.

6. Common problems

SymptomCause and fix
The client says the server has no authorization / /.well-known/… answers 404 oauth_unavailableOAuth is off: set AUTOXIDE_HTTP_PUBLIC_URL (no path) and AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OAUTH_CONSENT_URL, restart, check autoxide doctor. API endpoints answer auth.oauth_disabled.
The browser shows 400 with auth.oauth_client_invalidThe client metadata document could not be fetched or is not valid (it must be https, port 443, a public address, at most 5 KB, client_id equal to its own URL, no client secret), or dynamic registration is off and the client relies on it. The message gives the detail.
400 auth.oauth_redirect_invalidThe client’s redirect_uri is not one it registered. Ports are flexible only for 127.0.0.1 / [::1].
400 auth.oauth_request_invalidA parameter is missing or wrong (code_challenge_method must be S256, resource must be …/mcp, …/mcp/<module> or …/api/v1 of this server).
The consent page gets 404 auth.oauth_request_not_foundMore than 10 minutes passed, or the request was already decided. Start connecting again from the client.
The consent page gets 403 auth.session_required / auth.oauth_staff_onlyCall with the person’s own signed-in session, not an API key; only staff accounts approve clients.
422 on approveA permission was not offered, days is outside 1 to AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OAUTH_GRANT_DAYS, or a sensitive permission needs reauth_token. The request still waits.
The client is signed out after a while, /token answers invalid_grantThe approval expired or was revoked, the person can no longer sign in, or the client refreshed twice at once (a reused refresh token revokes the approval). Connect again.
A tool answers 403 insufficient_scopeThe person has the permission but did not approve it for this client. Reconnect and approve it.
auth.oauth_rate_limitedToo many authorization requests from one address; wait a minute.

Connecting an AI agent over MCP

Vietnamese: mcp.vi.md. Examples use curl with API set to your server (export API=https://api.example.com), and the TypeScript SDK (sdk/typescript). They run as tests against every build, so they match the server of this version.

AI agents call Autoxide as tools through the Model Context Protocol at /mcp (Streamable HTTP). Each tool runs the same code as the matching REST endpoint, with the same permission: a tool can never do what REST with the same permission cannot.

1. Create a key with the least permissions

Give the agent its own API key, with only what its job needs. content.write_own lets it write drafts of its own; publishing stays with people.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token
# save: REFRESH=.data.refresh_token

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/api-keys" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"name":"Writing agent","permissions":["content.read","content.write_own"],"current_password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# expect: 201
# save: AGENT_KEY=.data.key

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/me" -H "Authorization: Bearer $AGENT_KEY"

2. Connect the client

When the server has OAuth sign-in on, clients that support it (Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, IDEs) connect with the address alone and the person approves them in your interface: see Connecting MCP clients with OAuth sign-in. The rest of this section connects with an API key, which works with every client.

Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http autoxide https://api.example.com/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer $AUTOXIDE_AGENT_KEY"

Other MCP clients take a Streamable HTTP server with a header, e.g.:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "autoxide": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://api.example.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${AUTOXIDE_AGENT_KEY}" }
    }
  }
}

An agent that works with one module only can connect to that module’s own endpoint, /mcp/<module> (for example https://api.example.com/mcp/content): same authentication and permissions, but only that module’s tools, resources and prompts, so the model does not have to read the descriptions of every tool on the server. /llms.txt links each module’s endpoint.

3. What the agent can do

tools/list shows only the tools the key’s permissions allow. Each description ends with the permission it needs, and annotations say whether a tool is read-only or destructive (clients ask before calling those). A deprecated tool says so in its description and in every result (_meta.autoxide/deprecation), with the tool to use instead.

Limits:

  • Requests with an API key share its rate limit (AUTOXIDE_HTTP_RATE_LIMIT_API_KEY_PER_MINUTE).
  • Every write lands in the audit log under the key.
  • AI results are suggestions and drafts that a person reviews; nothing an agent writes is published by itself.
  • Tool results have the same shape as REST: {"data": …}, or a page with pagination; errors carry the same code.

4. Resources and prompts

Besides tools, /mcp offers resources (read-only documents: resources/list, resources/read) and prompts (templates for common jobs: prompts/list, prompts/get). Both follow permissions like tools: a resource is listed only to callers with its permission, and a prompt only to callers who may call every tool it leads to. A resource or prompt the caller may not use answers exactly like one that does not exist.

Every signed-in caller can read autoxide://kernel/llms.txt (the same text as /llms.txt) and autoxide://kernel/openapi.json (the REST contract). Prompts never call anything by themselves: they return messages that tell the model which tools to call, and the user’s arguments come inside tags such as <topic>…</topic>, marked as data.

The resources and prompts of this version (docs/mcp-tools.json lists them too):

ResourcePermissionType
autoxide://comments/guidecomments.moderatetext/markdown
autoxide://content/guidecontent.readtext/markdown
autoxide://content/schema/entrycontent.readapplication/schema+json
autoxide://kernel/moduleskernel.modules.readapplication/json
PromptArgumentsLeads to
comments.moderate_queuelimitcomments.queue, comments.moderate
content.draft_posttopic (required), locale, audiencecontent.create_draft

5. Let the agent find its way: /llms.txt

/llms.txt is a public page in the llmstxt.org format: where the OpenAPI document and /mcp are, how to authenticate, the conventions every endpoint follows, the installed modules and the MCP prompts and resources. It is generated from the code when the server starts, so it always matches this version. Links are absolute when AUTOXIDE_HTTP_PUBLIC_URL is set.

curl -sS "$API/llms.txt"

Under each module, /llms.txt links its own OpenAPI document and MCP endpoint and names its tools. A module’s OpenAPI document holds only the endpoints under /api/v1/<module> and the schemas they use, with the same conventions as the whole document — enough to call that module correctly without loading the rest of the API:

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/openapi/content.json"

6. From the quickstart to a working agent

A walk-through on your own machine, from an empty directory to an assistant that answers questions about stock and sales. It starts from the Quickstart (compose.quickstart.yml), so the server is at http://127.0.0.1:8080.

1. Sign in and make a key for the assistant. Use the administrator’s password from the file the server wrote (docker compose -f compose.quickstart.yml exec autoxide autoxide initial-password). Give the key only what the assistant needs — here, reading stock, products, prices and reports, and drafting invoices:

API=http://127.0.0.1:8080
TOKEN=$(curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"<password from the log>"}' | jq -r .data.access_token)
curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/api-keys" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"name":"Desk assistant","permissions":["inventory.read","catalog.products.read","catalog.prices.read","reporting.read","analytics.read","invoices.write"],"current_password":"<password from the log>"}' \
  | jq -r .data.key

The key (axk1_…) is shown once: keep it in your password manager. Check what it may do with curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/me" -H "Authorization: Bearer axk1_…".

2. Connect the client.

Claude Desktop takes local (stdio) servers in its configuration file (Settings → Developer → Edit Config, claude_desktop_config.json). The mcp-remote bridge (needs Node.js) connects it to an HTTP server with a header:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "autoxide": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp", "--header", "Authorization:${AUTOXIDE_AUTH}"],
      "env": { "AUTOXIDE_AUTH": "Bearer axk1_…" }
    }
  }
}

Restart Claude Desktop; the tools appear under the tools icon of a new chat. (mcp-remote speaks plain HTTP only to localhost; a server elsewhere needs HTTPS.)

Cursor talks Streamable HTTP itself. In ~/.cursor/mcp.json (every project) or .cursor/mcp.json (one project — do not commit the key):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "autoxide": {
      "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:AUTOXIDE_AGENT_KEY}" }
    }
  }
}

Start Cursor with AUTOXIDE_AGENT_KEY=axk1_… in its environment, then check Settings → MCP: autoxide should list its tools. For a narrower assistant, connect to one module only, e.g. http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp/inventory.

3. Ask for real work. A fresh installation has no products or stock yet: add some first (the API reference at /api/docs after setting AUTOXIDE_HTTP_API_DOCS=true, or your own front end). Then ask in plain words; the model picks the tools, and the client shows each call before or after it runs.

You askTools the agent callsWhat you get
“Which products are running low? Group them by warehouse.”inventory.list_low_stock, then catalog.get_product for namesA list of variants under their reorder point, with the quantity on hand
“How many units of SKU TS-RED-M do we have, and where?”catalog.list_products (search), inventory.get_levelsStock per location: on hand, reserved, available
“Draft an invoice for Công ty ABC: 10 × TS-RED-M at the list price.”catalog.resolve_price, invoices.create_draftA draft invoice; a person reviews and issues it — the key has no permission to issue
“How did sales go last week compared with the week before?”reporting.summary, reporting.factsTotals and the change, from the reporting module’s facts
“Which pages brought the most visitors this month?”analytics.overview, analytics.top_pagesVisits and top pages of the website

What keeps this safe:

  • The key decides: tools/list shows only the tools its permissions allow, and a tool can never do more than REST with the same permission. The assistant above can read and draft; it cannot change stock, refund an order or issue an invoice.
  • Orders come from checkout, not from tools: there is no tool that places an order for a customer. An agent prepares drafts (invoices, content, replies) that people confirm.
  • Writes are safe to retry (idempotency) and every write is in the audit log under the key’s name (/api/v1/audit).
  • Remove the key when you are done: DELETE /api/v1/auth/api-keys/{id}.

Building a mobile or desktop app

Vietnamese: mobile.vi.md. Examples use curl with API set to your server (export API=https://api.example.com). They run as tests against every build, so they match the server of this version.

Autoxide is an API only: a phone app, a desktop app or a point-of-sale terminal calls the same endpoints as a website. This guide walks through what such an app needs, in the order you usually build it, and points to the guide with the details of each part.

1. Pick an SDK

The TypeScript SDK (sdk/typescript) is generated from the API contract (docs/openapi.json), so it always matches the server of the same version. Use it for web, React Native and Node. There are no official Swift, Kotlin or Dart SDKs (decision D-20261121-drop-mobile-sdk): for a native or Flutter app, generate a client from docs/openapi.json (also served at /api/v1/openapi.json) with the OpenAPI generator of your platform, or call the REST endpoints directly. Whatever the client, three rules hold for every call:

  • Send the access token in Authorization: Bearer ….
  • Send an Idempotency-Key header (a new random UUID per action, kept across retries) on writes: phones retry on bad networks — see Retrying safely.
  • Every error is a Problem with a stable code; show detail (send Accept-Language: vi for Vietnamese) and branch on code — see Reading errors.

2. Sign in and stay signed in

Sign in with email and password (or a passkey, or a sign-in link — see Signing in). Keep both tokens in the platform’s secure store (Keychain on Apple platforms, Keystore-backed storage on Android), never in plain preferences.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token
# save: REFRESH=.data.refresh_token

The access token lives expires_in seconds. Shortly before it expires, or when a call answers 401 with auth.token_expired, exchange the refresh token for a new pair. Each refresh token works once: save the new one before using the new access token. Refresh from one place in the app only (one in-flight refresh at a time); two screens refreshing with the same token look like a stolen token, and the server then ends the whole session.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/refresh" --json '{"refresh_token":"'"$REFRESH"'"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token
# save: REFRESH=.data.refresh_token

When the refresh answers 401 (auth.invalid_refresh_token, auth.refresh_token_reused), clear the tokens and show the sign-in screen. When signing out, send the refresh token to POST /api/v1/auth/logout, then delete both tokens and the push token of the device (section 4).

Programs without a person (a kiosk, a sync service) use an API key instead — see API keys.

3. Sign in with Google, Microsoft or GitHub (PKCE)

The server runs the OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow with PKCE for the app, and keeps the PKCE verifier, state and nonce itself: the app never holds a client secret. An administrator adds the provider with the app’s return address in redirect_uris — a claimed HTTPS link (Universal Link on iOS, App Link on Android, e.g. https://app.example.com/sign-in/callback) or a custom scheme of your app (com.example.app:/sign-in/callback). See Signing in with Google, Microsoft, GitHub or OpenID Connect.

  1. The app calls POST /api/v1/auth/oidc/{slug}/start with {"redirect_uri": "<the app's return address>"}.
  2. It opens authorization_url in the system’s sign-in browser — ASWebAuthenticationSession on Apple platforms, Custom Tabs on Android, flutter_web_auth_2 in Flutter — not in an embedded web view, which providers refuse.
  3. The provider sends the browser back to the return address with code and state. The app sends both, unchanged, to POST /api/v1/auth/oidc/{slug}/callback and gets the same answer as /login: tokens, or 202 with an mfa_token when two-step sign-in is on.

The list of providers the sign-in screen shows (this server has outside sign-in turned off, so it answers 404):

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/oidc/providers"
# expect: 404

4. Push notifications

After signing in, and whenever the operating system gives the app a new push token, register the device. Registering the same token again only updates it, so do it on every app start.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/notifications/me/device-tokens" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"platform":"ios","token":"apns-device-token-from-the-os","app_id":"com.example.app","locale":"vi"}'
# expect: 201
# save: DEVICE=.data.id
  • platform is ios (APNs token) or android (Firebase Cloud Messaging token); app_id is the bundle id or package name; locale (en, vi) picks the language of the messages.
  • GET /api/v1/notifications/me/device-tokens lists the user’s devices; DELETE /api/v1/notifications/me/device-tokens/{id} stops pushes to one — call it when signing out.
  • The server drops a token the push service reports as no longer valid; register again when the operating system hands out a new one.
  • Which messages reach the phone follows the user’s notification preferences (/api/v1/notifications/me/preferences); the same messages are in the in-app inbox (/api/v1/notifications/me/inbox). Sending needs a push provider (FCM, APNs) set up on the server; without one, devices are still registered.

5. Upload photos straight to storage

Do not send large photos through the API server. Ask for a signed upload link, send the bytes from the phone straight to S3, then complete the upload — see Uploading large files straight to storage. Compute size and sha256 of the exact bytes you will send (after resizing on the phone). This server keeps files on its own disk, so it answers 409 media.direct_upload_unavailable: the app then uploads through POST /api/v1/media (multipart) instead.

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/media/uploads" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: 0193e3a4-7b1c-7f00-9a51-6f2b8c0d4e11' \
  --json '{"name":"shelf.jpg","content_type":"image/jpeg","size":482113,"sha256":"9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08"}'
# expect: 409

On S3 the answer is 201 with url, method and headers: upload with exactly those (a background upload task on iOS, WorkManager on Android, so it survives the app going to the background), then POST /api/v1/media/uploads/{id}/complete.

6. Work offline

An app that must keep working without a network (a shop counter, a delivery app) keeps a copy of the records on the device and sends its writes later. The server lists the kinds of records that can be kept in sync — each module of the server adds its own (the sample notes module adds notes.notes; this server has none):

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/kernel/sync/resources" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Each kind has a list endpoint (path) and a change feed (changes). The loop:

  1. First time: read the list endpoint (with pagination), then GET <changes> without a cursor; keep the cursor of the last change you applied.
  2. Catching up: GET <changes>?cursor=<last cursor>. Each item is {id, cursor, deleted, version, data}: the record as it is now (apply it again safely), or deleted: true — remove it, also when the user lost access to it. Read pages until pagination.next_cursor is null.
  3. Too far behind: a cursor older than the server keeps changes (AUTOXIDE_SYNC_RETENTION_DAYS, 30 days by default) answers 410 sync_cursor_expired: drop the local copy and start again from step 1.
  4. Writing offline: queue each write on the device with its own idempotency_key and the version (ETag) of the record it changed. When the network is back, send the queue with POST /api/v1/kernel/sync/batch:
{
  "operations": [
    {
      "id": "w-1",
      "method": "PATCH",
      "path": "/api/v1/notes/0193f1c2-5a7e-7c3d-8e21-4b6f0a9d2c11",
      "idempotency_key": "w-1",
      "if_match": "\"3\"",
      "body": { "title": "Shelf B restocked" }
    }
  ]
}

Each write runs exactly as its REST endpoint would — same permissions, checks and answers — and gets its own result {id, status, etag, location, body}; a failed write does not stop the others. Sending the batch again (the answer was lost) does not repeat what was done, thanks to the kept idempotency_key. A result 412 means someone changed the record since: its body.current is the record on the server. Merge, or ask the user, and queue a new write with the new version — the server never merges for you.

7. Real-time events and live signals

Screens that must refresh as things happen subscribe to events. The server must set AUTOXIDE_EVENTS_STREAM=true (this one does not, so both endpoints answer 404 kernel.stream_disabled).

  • Server-Sent Events — GET /api/v1/kernel/events/stream: one-way, plain HTTP, the simplest choice. See Receiving events in real time.
  • WebSocket — GET /api/v1/kernel/events/ws: the same events, permissions and resuming, plus live signals the app sends (“typing”, “online”) in a topic such as a conversation. Use it for chat or a courier’s live position screen.
curl -sS "$API/api/v1/kernel/events/ws?names=content.*" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# expect: 404

Open the socket with the Authorization header (native WebSocket clients — URLSessionWebSocketTask, OkHttp, web_socket_channel — can set it), names in the query and, on reconnect, last_event_id. Every message is a JSON text frame:

→ {"type":"subscribe","names":"comments.*"}
← {"type":"subscribed","names":["comments.*","content.*"]}
← {"type":"event","event":{"id":"0193f1c2-…","name":"content.entry_published","occurred_at":"2026-11-18T09:30:00Z","subject":"content.entry:0193…","actor_kind":"user","payload":{…}}}
→ {"type":"ack","id":"0193f1c2-…"}
→ {"type":"join","topic":"conversation:0193f1d0-…"}
← {"type":"joined","topic":"conversation:0193f1d0-…","online":["0193e0aa-…"]}
→ {"type":"typing","topic":"conversation:0193f1d0-…"}
← {"type":"signal","topic":"conversation:0193f1d0-…","user_id":"0193e0aa-…","signal":"typing"}
  • The socket only takes control messages: subscribe, unsubscribe, ack, join, leave, typing, ping. Data is written over REST (or the sync batch); anything else answers {"type":"error","code":"kernel.ws_unknown_command"}.
  • Delivery is at least once: skip event ids you already handled. A reset message means what you missed is no longer kept — reload over REST.
  • Close codes: 4401 — the credentials no longer hold (the access token expired): refresh and reconnect; 4403 — the user may no longer receive any event named; 1012 — the server restarts: reconnect with last_event_id. Reconnect with a growing delay (1 s, 2 s, 4 s… up to a minute).
  • Live signals are not stored. A topic <kind>:<id> exists only when a module opens it (kernel.ws_unknown_topic otherwise), and you may join it only when you may read the record.
  • On a phone, close the socket when the app goes to the background and rely on push notifications (section 4); reopen it with last_event_id when the app comes back.

8. In-app purchases

When the app sells the tenant’s subscription through the App Store or Google Play, the store collects and keeps the money; the server checks each purchase with the store and puts the tenant on the linked plan. An administrator links store products to plans (PUT /api/v1/plans/store/products/{store}/{product_id}), and the server needs the store’s credentials.

  1. Buy the product with StoreKit 2 or Google Play Billing.
  2. Send what the store returned — the signed transaction (StoreKit 2) or the purchaseToken (Google Play), unchanged — with plans.billing.manage:
curl -sS "$API/api/v1/plans/store/purchases" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: 0193e3a4-7b1c-7f00-9a51-000000000002' \
  --json '{"store":"app_store","proof":"signed-transaction-from-storekit"}'
# expect: 422

Here you are signed in to the platform tenant, which no plan limits, so it answers 422 plans.platform_exempt; a customer’s tenant on a server without the store set up gets 503 plans.store_unavailable. On a configured server the answer is the tenant’s subscription. Sending the same purchase again changes nothing, so send it on every app start until the server confirms it (then finish the transaction in StoreKit / acknowledge it in Google Play). Renewals, expiry and refunds reach the server from the store itself (server notifications); the app does not report them. Users change or cancel the subscription in the store, not through the API.

Checklist

  • Tokens in the secure store; one refresh at a time; 401 after a refresh → sign-in screen.
  • Idempotency-Key on every write you may retry, kept across retries.
  • Push token registered on every start, deleted on sign-out.
  • Large files straight to storage.
  • Offline: change feed with a kept cursor, queued writes with if_match, 412 handled by the app.
  • WebSocket or SSE only while the app is in the foreground; reconnect with last_event_id.
  • Purchases sent to the server until confirmed.

Signing in with Google, Microsoft, GitHub or OpenID Connect

Vietnamese: oidc.vi.md. Examples use curl with API set to your server (export API=https://api.example.com). They run as tests against every build, so they match the server of this version.

People can sign in with an outside identity provider instead of a password: Google, Microsoft (Entra ID), GitHub, or any OpenID Connect issuer. Each tenant adds its own providers. Autoxide is only the client of the provider; your interface drives the browser.

It is off by default. The server operator turns it on with AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OIDC=true. Providers can be managed while it is off; signing in then answers 404 auth.oidc_disabled.

1. Register the application at the provider

Register a web application at the provider and note its client id and client secret. Give it your interface’s callback page as the redirect (return) address, e.g. https://app.example.com/sign-in/callback.

  • Google — Google Cloud console, APIs & Services → Credentials → OAuth client ID (type Web application). Scopes openid email profile.
  • Microsoft — Microsoft Entra admin center, App registrations → New registration, platform Web. Create a client secret under Certificates & secrets. To trust the email of work accounts, add the optional claim xms_edov to the ID token (Token configuration): without it, Autoxide never links by email for Microsoft, because Entra lets the email be changed without verifying it.
  • GitHub — Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps → New OAuth App. GitHub has no OpenID Connect: Autoxide reads the user’s id and their primary, verified email from the GitHub API.
  • Any OpenID Connect issuer (Keycloak, Auth0, Okta, Zitadel…) — the issuer must publish /.well-known/openid-configuration and sign ID tokens with RS256 or ES256.

2. Add the provider to the tenant

Needs the permission auth.oidc.manage (auth.oidc.read to only list them) and, to add or change a provider, a signed-in session: an API key cannot (auth.session_required). The client secret is stored encrypted and never shown again (has_secret tells whether one is stored).

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}'
# save: TOKEN=.data.access_token

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/oidc-providers" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"slug":"google","kind":"google","name":"Google","client_id":"1234.apps.googleusercontent.com","client_secret":"from-google","redirect_uris":["https://app.example.com/sign-in/callback"]}'
# expect: 201
  • kind oidc needs issuer. microsoft defaults to any work or school account (https://login.microsoftonline.com/organizations/v2.0); give https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0 to allow only your company. github with an issuer is a GitHub Enterprise Server.
  • redirect_uris: the exact pages the provider may send the browser back to. They are compared character by character.
  • allowed_email_domains: only these email domains may sign in.
  • allow_signup: someone without an account gets one on first sign-in — only if self-registration is open too (AUTOXIDE_AUTH_SELF_REGISTRATION for staff, the setting auth.customer_registration for realm customer), or the provider gives new accounts a role (default_role_id, at default_org_id), which is how a company lets its staff in with its own Entra ID. Whoever saves a provider that gives a role must be able to give that role themselves, on every save. At each sign-up the server checks again that the person who last saved the provider is still active, still holds auth.oidc.manage and can still give that role; otherwise sign-up is refused (auth.oidc_default_role_unavailable) until an administrator saves the provider again.
  • The provider address must be public: addresses on private networks are refused unless the operator sets AUTOXIDE_AUTH_OIDC_ALLOW_PRIVATE_NETWORKS=true (for tests only).

Change it with PATCH /api/v1/auth/oidc-providers/{id} and remove it with DELETE (every account link to it goes too).

3. Sign in

The interface lists the buttons from GET /api/v1/auth/oidc/providers (public). This example server has outside sign-in off:

curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/oidc/providers"
# expect: 404

Then, with outside sign-in on:

  1. POST /api/v1/auth/oidc/{slug}/start with {"redirect_uri": "https://app.example.com/sign-in/callback"} answers authorization_url. Open it in the browser. The server keeps the PKCE verifier, state and nonce for 10 minutes; they never leave it.
  2. The provider sends the browser back to your page with code and state in the query.
  3. POST /api/v1/auth/oidc/{slug}/callback with {"code": "…", "state": "…"} answers exactly like POST /api/v1/auth/login: tokens, or 202 with an mfa_token when the account has two-step sign-in (continue with POST /api/v1/auth/login/mfa). The state works once.

Which account signs in:

  • the account already linked to this provider identity;
  • otherwise the account with the same email — only when both the provider and Autoxide have verified it; if either has not, the answer is 409 auth.oidc_link_required: sign in the usual way and link the provider (below). This stops someone from taking over an account created in advance with another person’s email;
  • otherwise a new account, when allowed (see allow_signup), else 403 auth.oidc_signup_closed. An unverified email never creates an account (403 auth.oidc_email_unverified).

Errors: 400 auth.oidc_state_invalid (start again), 401 auth.oidc_token_invalid with reason (signature, issuer, audience, expired, nonce, unknown_key, algorithm…), 403 auth.oidc_email_domain_not_allowed, 503 auth.oidc_provider_unavailable.

4. Link and unlink in the account

  • GET /api/v1/auth/me/identities lists the linked providers.
  • POST /api/v1/auth/me/identities/{slug}/start with redirect_uri and your current_password (or a reauth_token from POST /api/v1/auth/me/reauth), then POST /api/v1/auth/me/identities/{slug}/callback with code and state, signed in with the same session.
  • DELETE /api/v1/auth/me/identities/{id} removes a link, but not your last way to sign in (409 auth.identity_last_method): set a password or add a passkey first.

Linked identities (provider subject and email) are part of the account’s personal data export and are deleted with the account.

Signing in with Google or GitHub does not replace the phone-number verification some modules require for posting content (Vietnamese Decree 147/2024/ND-CP).

Adding blocks for pages built from blocks

Pages built from blocks (step 67) are trees of blocks: sections, headings, images, a product grid, a form. A person drags them in an interface, or the AI page builder assembles them from a description; both edit the same JSON layout. Every block is declared by a module. This guide is for developers who add blocks to a module, so that a shop owner can put the module’s features on any page.

Vietnamese: page-blocks.vi.md.

The rules

  1. A block is data, not code. It has a name, a group, a label, one sentence for the AI and a JSON Schema of its props. The website draws it; the server checks it. There is no way for a block to carry HTML, CSS or a script.
  2. The name is <module>.<block>, e.g. catalog.product_grid, forms.embed. The label and the AI hint are English sentences, translated in the module’s locales/vi.json under text:<sentence>; cargo xtask check refuses a sentence without a translation.
  3. The props schema is the only check. It uses a small part of JSON Schema that the server checks itself (see “Props” below). Every object is closed (additionalProperties: false), so a page cannot hide anything the schema does not describe.
  4. Prices, stock and dates of a sale come from data, never from text. A block that shows them declares with_data() and returns the current values when the page is read. The AI is told never to write them into text.
  5. Changing a block is like changing an API (D-059): adding an optional prop is fine; removing a prop or changing its meaning is a new block (…_v2), and the old one keeps working.

1. Declare the block

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use autoxide_kernel::blocks::{BlockCategory, BlockType};

pub(crate) const PRODUCT_GRID: BlockType = BlockType::new(
    "shop.product_grid",
    BlockCategory::Commerce,
    "Product grid",
    "Use to show several products of a collection with their current prices; never write prices into text.",
    r#"{
        "type": "object",
        "additionalProperties": false,
        "required": ["collection_id"],
        "properties": {
            "collection_id": {"type": "string", "format": "uuid"},
            "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 24},
            "columns": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 6, "x-responsive": true}
        }
    }"#,
)
.with_data();
}

Then return it from the module, next to its permissions and events:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Module for ShopModule {
    fn blocks(&self) -> Vec<autoxide_kernel::blocks::BlockType> {
        vec![PRODUCT_GRID]
    }
    // …
}
}

with_children() makes a block that holds other blocks (a section, columns, tabs). requires(feature) limits it to tenants whose plan has a feature the module declares. A wrong name, a schema the server cannot check or a missing translation stops the program at start, not at run time.

2. Props

The schema accepts type, properties, required, additionalProperties, items, enum, const, minLength / maxLength, minimum / maximum, minItems / maxItems, format (uuid, date-time), title, description, default, examples, and three keywords of Autoxide:

KeywordMeaning
x-responsive: trueThe value is one value, or {"base": …, "md": …, "lg": …} by screen size.
x-media: trueThe string is the id of a media item (an image or a video of the media module), never a URL.
x-link: trueA link with the rules of post bodies: https://, http://, mailto:, tel: or a path on the site (/…); never javascript:.

Any other keyword is an error at start. Strings that look like HTML tags are refused. Colors are theme tokens ("primary"), never color codes, so a page keeps the brand when the theme changes.

3. Data at read time

A block declared with_data() must give its data when a public page is read. Register a BlockData in Module::start:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::sync::Arc;

use autoxide_kernel::blocks::{BlockData, BlockRef, BlockRequest};
use autoxide_kernel::error::Error;
use serde_json::Value;

pub(crate) struct Grids(pub(crate) Arc<ShopService>);

#[async_trait::async_trait]
impl BlockData for Grids {
    async fn resolve(
        &self,
        request: &BlockRequest<'_>,
        _block: &str,
        items: &[BlockRef],
    ) -> Result<Vec<Option<Value>>, Error> {
        // One query for every grid of the page, filtered like the module's public endpoints.
        let ids: Vec<String> = items
            .iter()
            .filter_map(|item| item.props["collection_id"].as_str().map(str::to_owned))
            .collect();
        let found = self.0.public_collections(request.tenant, request.site, request.locale, &ids).await?;
        Ok(items
            .iter()
            .map(|item| {
                let id = item.props["collection_id"].as_str()?;
                found.get(id).cloned()
            })
            .collect())
    }
}
}
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn start(&mut self, context: &mut StartContext<'_>) -> Result<(), Error> {
    // …
    context.block_data(PRODUCT_GRID.name, Arc::new(Grids(service.clone())))?;
    Ok(())
}
}
  • resolve is called once per block type per page, with every block of that type: read them all in one query. Return one item per block, in the same order.
  • Return only public data, filtered by request.site (the website being read) and request.locale. A record that is no longer public is None: the website hides that block and the page still shows.
  • An error or a slow answer (over 2 seconds) turns only your blocks into null; the page still answers.
  • The page is read through GET /api/v1/content/public/resolve; your data is in blocks_data, by block id.

4. What the AI sees

The AI page builder receives the list of blocks the tenant can use: each name, the AI hint and the props schema. Write the hint as one sentence saying when to use the block and what it must not be used for. Keep props few and named plainly; give description to props whose meaning is not obvious. Whatever the AI answers goes through the same checks as a person’s layout.

5. Test it

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[tokio::test]
async fn grid_returns_current_prices() {
    TestDatabase::run(async |test| {
        let app = TestApp::builder(test).module(shop_module()).build().await.unwrap();
        // … create a public collection …
        let tenant = app.default_tenant();
        let site = autoxide_kernel::tenancy::Site::whole(&tenant);
        let request = autoxide_kernel::blocks::BlockRequest::new(&tenant, &site, "en");
        let grid = autoxide_kernel::blocks::BlockRef::new("g1", serde_json::json!({"collection_id": collection}));
        let data = app.blocks().resolve(&request, &[("shop.product_grid", grid)]).await;
