The new folder builds and passes its tests at once; it also has a README.md + README.vi.md, an AGENTS.md with the rules for AI agents working in it (CLAUDE.md links to it, and short versions for Cursor and Copilot sit in .cursor/rules/ and .github/copilot-instructions.md), and .github/workflows/ci.yml, which runs check.sh on SQLite and PostgreSQL once you push it. Add --core-path <checkout> to depend on a local checkout of Autoxide instead of the release tag (to try a change of the core).

acme/
├── Cargo.toml          the workspace
├── rust-toolchain.toml
├── clippy.toml
├── check.sh            format, lints, tests on both databases
├── README.md, README.vi.md
├── AGENTS.md           rules for AI agents (CLAUDE.md links to it)
├── .github/workflows/ci.yml
├── bookmarks/          your module: crate `acme-bookmarks`
│   ├── Cargo.toml
│   ├── locales/vi.json
│   └── src/
└── server/             your server: crate `acme-server`, binary `acme`
    ├── Cargo.toml
    └── src/main.rs

The workspace Cargo.toml names the core once. Depend on a release tag, so that your build does not change until you choose a newer release:

[workspace]
resolver = "3"
members = ["bookmarks", "server"]

[workspace.dependencies]
autoxide = { git = "https://github.com/thuongtamduy/autoxide", tag = "vX.Y.Z" }
autoxide-kernel = { git = "https://github.com/thuongtamduy/autoxide", tag = "vX.Y.Z" }
autoxide-testkit = { git = "https://github.com/thuongtamduy/autoxide", tag = "vX.Y.Z" }

async-trait = "0.1"
axum = "0.8"
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros"] }
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
tracing = "0.1"
utoipa = "6.0"
utoipa-axum = "0.3"
uuid = { version = "1", features = ["v7"] }
validator = { version = "0.21", features = ["derive"] }

Three things to know:

  • All three core crates use the same tag. Cargo then builds one copy of the kernel; two tags would give two kernels whose types do not match.
  • The libraries below the core are part of the module contract (axum, sea-orm, utoipa…): keep the major versions of the release you build on — the table “Stability of the module contract” in MODULE_GUIDE.md lists them. The core turns on the features it needs (database drivers, the async runtime); you add only what your code uses. For sea-orm, turn the default features off as above.
  • Library versions. A git dependency does not bring the core’s Cargo.lock: cargo picks the newest compatible version of every library. To start from exactly the versions the release was tested with, copy the Cargo.lock of the tag into your repository before the first build (cargo trims what you do not use). Commit your Cargo.lock.

The example’s Cargo.toml also sets the lints of the core (no unsafe, no unwrap outside tests) and a build profile that keeps test programs small; copy both, with clippy.toml.

2. The module crate

bookmarks/Cargo.toml lists what the module’s code uses; the test kit is a dev-dependency:

[package]
name = "acme-bookmarks"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
async-trait.workspace = true
autoxide-kernel.workspace = true
axum.workspace = true
sea-orm.workspace = true
serde.workspace = true
serde_json.workspace = true
tracing.workspace = true
utoipa.workspace = true
utoipa-axum.workspace = true
uuid.workspace = true
validator.workspace = true

[dev-dependencies]
autoxide-testkit.workspace = true
tokio.workspace = true

The module’s name — here bookmarks — is the prefix of everything it owns: tables bookmarks_…, routes under /api/v1/bookmarks, permissions, events, jobs, error codes and MCP tools named bookmarks.…. Choose a name no official module has.

A module crate shows exactly two things to other crates: pub mod api (traits and types other modules may use) and pub fn module(). Everything else is private. Start with one file per role:

FileWhat it holds
src/lib.rsthe Module implementation: what the module declares to the core
src/api.rsthe contract for other modules
src/config.rssettings
src/migration/tables
src/entity.rsthe SeaORM entity of each table
src/permissions.rspermissions
src/events.rsevents
src/service.rsall the logic
src/http.rsREST handlers
src/tools.rsMCP tools
src/retention.rsa scheduled background job
locales/vi.jsonVietnamese texts
src/tests.rstests

lib.rs is the table of contents. Every function of Module except name has a default, so a module declares only what it has:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub mod api;
// … private modules …

pub fn module() -> impl Module {
    BookmarksModule::default()
}

impl Module for BookmarksModule {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str {
        "bookmarks"
    }

    fn configure(&mut self, reader: &mut ConfigReader<'_>) -> Result<(), Invalid> {
        self.config = Some(BookmarksConfig::read(reader)?);
        Ok(())
    }

    fn migrations(&self) -> Vec<Box<dyn MigrationTrait>> {
        migration::all()
    }

    fn permissions(&self) -> Vec<Permission> {
        permissions::all()
    }

    fn start(&mut self, context: &mut StartContext<'_>) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let config = self.config.clone().unwrap_or_default();
        let service = Arc::new(BookmarkService::new(context.outbox()?, config));
        self.service = Some(service.clone());
        context.provide::<dyn api::Bookmarks>(service)
    }

    fn routes(&self) -> OpenApiRouter {
        self.service.clone().map_or_else(OpenApiRouter::new, http::routes)
    }

    // … events, translations, subscriptions, jobs, schedules, tools …
}
}

The rules that matter most, each shown in the example file named:

  • Tables (migration/, entity.rs): named bookmarks_…; ids are UUIDv7 made in the application; a table that holds a customer’s data has a tenant_id column, and every key and index starts with it; no foreign key to a table of another module — keep the id only. Migrations are written with the schema builder, not SQL, so one migration runs on both databases, and each has a down. A released migration is never edited: add a new one.

  • Helper tables (migration/mod.rs): Outbox::record needs a bookmarks_events table and the job queue a bookmarks_jobs table. Do not write them yourself — the kernel defines them, and one call adds both in their current shape after your own migrations:

    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use autoxide_kernel::migration::{HelperTable, helper_tables};

pub(crate) fn all() -> Vec<Box<dyn MigrationTrait>> {
    let mut migrations: Vec<Box<dyn MigrationTrait>> =
        vec![Box::new(m0001_create_bookmark::Migration)];
    migrations.extend(helper_tables("bookmarks", &[HelperTable::Events, HelperTable::Jobs]));
    migrations
}
}

    Ask only for what the module uses (&[HelperTable::Events] for a module without jobs). Each helper table is its own chain of migrations with fixed names, so a table you need later is one more call at the end of the list, never a change to an earlier one. The official modules of the core keep their older step-by-step lists, because those names are already recorded in existing databases.

  • Logic in the service (service.rs): every method takes the TenantContext of the customer, reads through tenant.database().read(), writes in one short begin_write() transaction, and filters every query with .scoped(tenant). A write records its event in the same transaction (Outbox::record).

  • Handlers and tools only call the service (http.rs, tools.rs): take the input (ValidJson<T>), check the permission (principal.require(&BOOKMARKS_WRITE)?), call one service method, return Data<T>, Page<T> or Created<T>. Routes are registered with routes!, which puts them in the OpenAPI document; the /// comment and every response description are copied there, so write them in English for the API’s callers.

  • Errors carry a stable code with the module prefix (bookmarks.url_taken) and an English text; the Vietnamese text goes under the same code in locales/vi.json.

  • Settings (config.rs) are declared once with Setting and read through ConfigReader, never std::env::var. Use a prefix of your own (ACME_…); AUTOXIDE_… belongs to the core.

  • Both databases, always. Do not use a type, function or syntax only one of them has.

3. The server

server/Cargo.toml:

[package]
name = "acme-server"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[[bin]]
name = "acme"
path = "src/main.rs"

[dependencies]
acme-bookmarks = { path = "../bookmarks" }
autoxide.workspace = true

server/src/main.rs is the whole program:

use std::process::ExitCode;

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    autoxide::Autoxide::new()
        .name("acme")
        .version(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
        .module(acme_bookmarks::module)
        .run()
}

Autoxide::new() is the official program with every official module; .module(…) adds yours, one line each. Your modules start after the official ones, in the order added, so they can require any trait an official module provides, and a module of yours that uses another of yours comes after it. .run() gives the binary the standard command line.

4. Run it

From the workspace directory. The first build compiles the whole core and takes a while.

cargo run -p acme-server -- config                # every setting, yours included; checks them
cargo run -p acme-server -- migrate up            # creates the tables of every module, yours included
AUTOXIDE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL=admin@example.com \
AUTOXIDE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD='correct horse battery staple' \
  cargo run -p acme-server -- serve               # http://127.0.0.1:8080; creates the first administrator

Which modules run is a setting, AUTOXIDE_MODULES (see docs/MODULES.md): by default every official module and every module you added; AUTOXIDE_MODULES=official,-bookmarks turns yours off, and a module turned on brings the modules it names in Module::depends_on. acme modules lists every module with its tier, whether it is on, and what it depends on (--json for programs). acme openapi and acme mcp-manifest always print the full contract.

With no settings the server keeps its data in SQLite under ./data. For PostgreSQL set DATABASE_URL=postgres://…; nothing else changes. acme config --env-example > .env.example writes a documented list of every setting, and acme doctor checks an installation step by step.

In another terminal, sign in and call your module. The administrator created on first start holds every permission, including the ones your module declares:

export API=http://127.0.0.1:8080
TOKEN=$(curl -sS "$API/api/v1/auth/login" \
  --json '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}' \
  | sed -n 's/.*"access_token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
curl -sS "$API/api/v1/bookmarks" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --json '{"url":"https://www.rust-lang.org/","title":"Rust"}'
curl -sS "$API/api/v1/bookmarks" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Your routes are in the API document at $API/api/v1/openapi.json (also acme openapi), your tools in acme mcp-manifest and at the MCP endpoint, and everything the module declares is listed at GET /api/v1/kernel/modules.

5. Tests on both databases

Tests get an empty database each from TestDatabase::run; TestApp builds your module the way the server does and calls it over REST and with a real MCP client:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[tokio::test]
async fn a_bookmark_can_be_created() {
    TestDatabase::run(async |test| {
        let app = TestApp::builder(test)
            .user("ada", 0xada, &["bookmarks.read", "bookmarks.write"])
            .module(crate::module())
            .build()
            .await
            .unwrap();
        let answer = app
            .post("/api/v1/bookmarks")
            .token("ada")
            .json(json!({"url": "https://www.rust-lang.org/", "title": "Rust"}))
            .send()
            .await
            .unwrap();
        assert_eq!(answer.status(), StatusCode::CREATED);
    })
    .await
    .unwrap();
}
}

The database is chosen by TEST_DATABASE_URL: unset is SQLite, a postgres:// URL is PostgreSQL. Run every test on both:

cargo test --workspace
TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/postgres \
  cargo test --workspace -- --test-threads=4

src/tests.rs of the example shows the tests a module should have: REST and MCP give the same result, permissions are checked, a concurrent write (two requests keeping the same link) lets one through, two tenants never see each other (leak_check), the tables follow the rules (schema_ownership_violations, schema_tenancy_violations), the job and the settings work. server/tests/cli.rs runs the real binary: migrate up, openapi and mcp-manifest include the module. check.sh runs format, lints and both test runs; keep a script like it and run it in CI.

Fakes of other modules

When your module calls a trait another module publishes, test it against that module’s fake instead of copying one. A module ships its fakes in api::testing behind the testing feature; enable it only for tests:

[dev-dependencies]
autoxide-ledger = { git = "https://github.com/thuongtamduy/autoxide", tag = "vX.Y.Z", features = ["testing"] }

autoxide_ledger::api::testing::FakeLedger keeps entries, payments and refunds in memory with the same replay rules as the real ledger. Register ledger.module() before your module, read what your module did (entries(), payments(), refunds(), balance), and report a payment as collected with ledger.succeed(&tenant, &payment) — it writes ledger.payment_succeeded to the outbox like the real ledger, so your listener runs once you drain the dispatcher.

The same pattern exists for the other traits modules most often call: autoxide_notifications::api::testing::FakeNotifier (keeps what your module sent — sent() with the real dedupe_key rule, calls() with every call, kinds() declared) and autoxide_compliance::api::testing::FakeConsentLedger (consents in memory with the real “broader key” rule; set them up with allow / deny, read them back with state_of / records, make the ledger fail with set_failing).

autoxide_testkit::FakeMailer keeps the mails your module sends (sent(), to(address), calls()) with the real dedupe_key rule, and autoxide_address::api::testing::FakeAdministrativeUnits holds a few provinces and communes (sample(), or your own with province / commune / expired_commune) so addresses validate like the real address module.

autoxide_media::api::testing::FakeMedia is a media library in memory: add(public) / add_with / insert items, upload(user) for an item someone uploaded, set_alt(id, locale, alt), set_ai_image, remove; IDs it does not hold are not returned, like the real media module.

autoxide_catalog::api::testing::FakeCatalog holds variants (build one with variant(id, org) and change what your tests need, then insert_variant), a price history per variant (set_price, push_price, set_price_history; current and reference prices follow it like the real catalog), price floors, bundles and display prices, and it accepts a sale-price source (CatalogExtensions).

6. The rules of the core, checked on your crate

Inside the Autoxide repository, cargo xtask check enforces the module rules. For a crate anywhere else, run the same source rules from a checkout of Autoxide at the tag you build on:

cargo run --manifest-path /path/to/autoxide/xtask/Cargo.toml -- check-module /path/to/acme/bookmarks

It checks: the crate exposes only pub mod api and pub fn module; api does not reach into the crate’s internals; routes go through routes!; handlers and tools do not touch the database; safety lints are not switched off in src/; settings are not read with std::env::var; hand-written SQL is built with autoxide_kernel::database::statement; every error code and description has a Vietnamese text; entities have tenant_id; queries are filtered by tenant; MCP tools pass the caller to the service where REST limits by scope.

What it cannot see lives in the database and is checked by your tests (step 5): the table prefix, no foreign key to another module, tenant_id first in every key and index, no data crossing tenants.

7. Upgrading to a newer Autoxide

  1. Read CHANGELOG.md of the new release: breaking changes for modules are under Changed and Removed, the Rust items under ### Breaking (Rust).
  2. Change the tag in your workspace Cargo.toml (all three core crates) and build: cargo updates Cargo.lock for the core crates. Run your tests on both databases.
  3. On each server: acme migrate up, then start the new binary — as for the official server (docs/DEPLOY.md).

What the core promises: while its version is 0.x, a breaking change to the module contract comes only in a minor release (0.17 → 0.18), never in a patch release; an item that is going away is #[deprecated] for at least one minor release first; the Module trait only grows by functions with a default body. From 1.0 the contract follows Semantic Versioning. The full statement is in MODULE_GUIDE.md, “Stability of the module contract”.

The core crates are not on crates.io yet; until they are, the git tag is the way to depend on them.

Checklist

  • The module crate exposes only pub mod api and pub fn module
  • Tables named <module>_…, UUIDv7 ids, tenant_id first in every key and index, migrations with down; event and job tables from helper_tables
  • Permissions declared; every handler and tool requires one
  • Logic only in the service; each write records its event in the same transaction
  • Every route documented: summary, permission, every response
  • MCP tools for what agents should be able to do
  • Error codes prefixed with the module name and translated
  • Data about a user deleted on USER_DELETED
  • Holding personal data? Implement Module::dormant too: register the same export part (context.personal_data) and USER_DELETED handler (context.on_user_deleted), built without your service, so a turned-off module still exports and deletes a person’s data (see modules/notes/src/lib.rs)
  • Settings with a prefix of your own, declared with Setting
  • Tests on SQLite and PostgreSQL, including concurrent writes, tenant isolation and the table rules
  • cargo xtask check-module reports no violations

Sending SMS through eSMS

The esms module sends one-time codes and customer-care SMS through eSMS, a Vietnamese SMS brandname provider. Each tenant uses its own eSMS account and brandname.

Experimental. This adapter was written from the provider’s public documentation (https://developers.esms.vn, read on 2026-11-21) and is not yet verified against the live service. Test it with the eSMS test environment (below) before relying on it.

Vietnamese: esms.vi.md.

What it does, and what it does not
One-time codes (phone verification, sign-in, order and booking codes)sent as eSMS customer-care messages (SmsType 2)
Transactional notices of the notifications modulesent the same way
Advertising messagesrefused with esms.marketing_unsupported
Numbers outside Vietnam (not +84)refused with esms.phone_unsupported
Delivery reports (did the message reach the phone)not read; an accepted message means eSMS took it

Advertising SMS in Vietnam needs prior consent, the do-not-call list, permitted hours and an advertising brandname (Decree 91/2020/ND-CP; check the original text or ask a legal professional). eSMS has a separate bulk function for it that takes at least 30 numbers per request. The adapter does not send advertising through the customer-care route.

1. For the operator: turn the module on

The module is experimental, so it is off until named:

AUTOXIDE_MODULES=official,esms

AUTOXIDE_ESMS_API_URL (default https://rest.esms.vn) only needs changing to point at a test server. There is no server-wide eSMS account.

When the module is on, every tenant sends SMS through its own eSMS account; a tenant that has not set one gets the error provider.not_configured where an SMS would be sent.

2. For the tenant: what to get from eSMS

  1. Register at esms.vn and sign in.
  2. Open API management (“Quản lý API”) and copy the ApiKey and the SecretKey.
  3. Ask eSMS to register your brandname for customer-care messages, and the message templates you will send. The mobile networks only deliver customer-care messages that match a registered template; anything else is refused (esms.template_rejected).
  4. If eSMS restricts your account by IP address, give them the address of your Autoxide server (otherwise: esms.ip_not_allowed).

Every SMS that carries a one-time code has a default text, and a tenant setting that replaces it so it matches the template you registered (group sms_template, list them with GET /api/v1/kernel/settings?group=sms_template). Register either the default text (replace the parts in braces by the variable syntax eSMS asks for) or your own text, then set your text in the setting:

Used forSettingDefault textPlaceholders
Phone verificationcompliance.sms_template.phone_verificationMa xac thuc cua ban: {code}. Het han sau {minutes} phut. Khong chia se ma nay.{code}, {minutes}
Sign-in by phonecompliance.sms_template.sign_inMa dang nhap cua ban: {code}. Het han sau {minutes} phut. Khong chia se ma nay.{code}, {minutes}
Booking code (bookings)bookings.sms_template.guest_codeYour booking code is {code}. It expires in {minutes} minutes.{code}, {minutes}
Guest order lookup (orders)orders.sms_template.order_lookupYour code to view order {number} is {code}. It expires in {minutes} minutes. (translated to the order’s language){code}, {number}, {minutes}
Guest address change (orders)orders.sms_template.address_changeYour code to change the delivery address of order {number} is {code}. It expires in {minutes} minutes. (translated){code}, {number}, {minutes}
Notices (notifications)—the texts of your own templates in that module—
 
curl -X PUT https://your-server/api/v1/kernel/settings/compliance.sms_template.sign_in \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"value": "[MYSHOP] {code} la ma dang nhap cua ban, hieu luc {minutes} phut"}'

A template must contain {code} exactly once and only the placeholders of its message (otherwise 422, error on value). Your text is sent as is, whatever the buyer’s language. DELETE the setting to go back to the default text.

3. For the tenant: enter the account

All calls need the permission kernel.settings.manage. Secrets are set over REST only; they are stored encrypted and never returned.

curl -X PUT https://your-server/api/v1/kernel/settings/esms.connection.sms.api_key \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"value": "YOUR_API_KEY"}'
SettingSecretValue
esms.connection.sms.api_keyyesApiKey
esms.connection.sms.secret_keyyesSecretKey
esms.connection.sms.brandnamenoyour registered brandname
esms.connection.sms.environmentnosandbox to use the eSMS test environment: nothing is delivered or charged. Unset or production: real messages.

GET /api/v1/kernel/settings?group=connection shows which fields are set, when the connection was last used and its last error.

4. Test the connection

curl -X POST https://your-server/api/v1/kernel/settings/esms.connection.sms.api_key/test \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

This asks eSMS for the account balance (the balance itself is not returned). "ok": true means the ApiKey and SecretKey are accepted. It does not check the brandname or the templates: for that, set esms.connection.sms.environment to sandbox, trigger a code, and read the connection’s last error.

eSMS has no separate sandbox address or sandbox account: the test environment is the same API and the same ApiKey / SecretKey, with a Sandbox flag the adapter adds to each request. Set the setting back to production (or remove it) to send real messages.

Webhook

None. The adapter does not use the eSMS status callback (it carries no signature), so there is no address to paste into eSMS.

Errors

CodeMeaningRetry
provider.not_configuredthis tenant has not set the named settingafter setting it
esms.credentials_rejectedwrong ApiKey / SecretKey (eSMS 101)after fixing
esms.insufficient_balancenot enough balance (eSMS 103)yes, after topping up
esms.brandname_rejectedbrandname unknown or not active (eSMS 104)after fixing
esms.template_rejectedtext matches no registered template (eSMS 146)after registering
esms.carrier_not_registeredbrandname not registered with that mobile network (eSMS 177)after registering
esms.phone_rejectednumber malformed or blocked (eSMS 99, 108)no
esms.content_blockedtext contains a blocked keyword (eSMS 201)no
esms.ip_not_allowedserver IP not on the eSMS allow list (eSMS 140)after eSMS adds it
esms.account_inactiveaccount not activated or locked (eSMS 143)after eSMS unlocks it
esms.request_rejectedany other eSMS code; the message names itno
esms.unavailableeSMS did not answer or answered with a server erroryes
esms.marketing_unsupported, esms.phone_unsupportedsee the table at the topno

A message sent again with the same reference is not delivered twice: the reference is passed as the eSMS RequestId, which eSMS refuses to repeat for 24 hours.

Phone numbers and message texts are never written to logs.

Giao Hang Nhanh (GHN)

Connect a tenant’s own Giao Hang Nhanh account to Autoxide shipping: shipping fees at checkout, bookings, labels, cancellation and delivery status.

Vietnamese: ghn.vi.md.

Experimental. This connector is written from GHN’s public documentation (https://developer.ghn.vn, read on 2026-11-21); it is not yet verified against the live service. Try it with a GHN staging account first. The points that still need a real account are listed under Not verified yet.

For the person who runs the server

The module is off by default. Turn it on by name; shipping comes with it:

AUTOXIDE_MODULES=official,ghn
SettingDefaultMeaning
AUTOXIDE_GHN_API_URLhttps://online-gateway.ghn.vnGHN API for live accounts
AUTOXIDE_GHN_SANDBOX_API_URLhttps://dev-online-gateway.ghn.vnGHN staging API, for accounts marked sandbox

There is no setting for a GHN token: every tenant uses its own account. If your GHN token has an allowed-IP list, add the public IP of this server to it.

What the tenant needs from GHN

  1. Sign in at https://developer.ghn.vn (staging: https://developer.ghn.dev) with the phone number of the GHN account.
  2. Account menu → Manage token: reveal the Token API (GHN sends an OTP to the phone) and copy it.
  3. Note the ShopId of the shop that ships the parcels (shown in the account information). Parcels are picked up at the address of that shop.

Staging and production are separate accounts with separate tokens.

Connect the account

Needs the permission shipping.carriers.manage. The token is stored encrypted and is never returned.

POST /api/v1/shipping/carrier-accounts
{
  "carrier_code": "ghn",
  "name": "GHN main shop",
  "credentials": { "token": "<Token API>" },
  "settings": { "shop_id": 196560 },
  "sandbox": false
}

sandbox: true is for a token from https://developer.ghn.dev. Optional settings:

SettingDefaultMeaning
required_noteKHONGCHOXEMHANGDelivery instruction: KHONGCHOXEMHANG (do not open), CHOXEMHANGKHONGTHU (may look), CHOTHUHANG (may try)
payment_type_id1Who pays GHN’s fee: 1 the shop, 2 the recipient
label_sizea5Label page: a5, 80x80 or 52x70
contentHàng hóaDescription of the goods sent to GHN

The answer holds webhook_path once — keep it for the next step.

Then test the connection: POST /api/v1/shipping/carrier-accounts/{id}/test. check_status becomes ok, or failed with check_error_code:

CodeWhat to do
shipping.carrier_unauthorizedGHN refused the token (wrong token, wrong environment, or this server’s IP is not in the allowed list)
ghn.shop_not_foundThe token does not manage this ShopId, or the shop is locked
ghn.account_incompletetoken or shop_id is missing
shipping.carrier_unavailableGHN did not answer; try again

Finally create a shipping method of kind carrier with this carrier_account_id (see docs/SHIPPING.md). service_code is 2 (light goods, under 20 kg), 5 (heavy goods or several parcels), or empty to choose by weight and number of parcels.

Status webhook

  1. Build the full address: the public address of your Autoxide server + webhook_path, for example https://api.example.com/api/v1/shipping/webhooks/ghn/<hook>/<token>.
  2. In the GHN Developer Portal: account menu → Webhook configuration → tab Order → paste the address → Create webhook. GHN needs about 15 minutes to apply a change.

Treat the address as a secret: GHN does not sign its callbacks, so the address is what proves a callback belongs to this account. Autoxide also checks that the ShopID in the callback is the shop of the account, and answers 401 otherwise. If the address leaks, create a new carrier account (new address) and turn the old one off.

Repeated callbacks are applied once. Only status changes are used; fee, weight and COD-transfer callbacks are accepted and ignored.

How GHN statuses appear

GHNAutoxide
ready_to_pick, picking, money_collect_pickingready_to_ship
pickedpicked_up
storing, sorting, transportingin_transit
delivering, money_collect_deliveringout_for_delivery
delivereddelivered
delivery_faildelivery_failed
waiting_to_return, return, return_transporting, return_sorting, returning, return_failreturning
returnedreturned
cancelcancelled
lost, damage, scraplost
exceptionnot applied (handle it with GHN)

The original GHN status is kept as carrier_status on each tracking event.

Limits

  • Addresses are sent in Vietnam’s two-level model in force since 2025-07-01 (province + ward/commune, by name). The old district-based codes of GHN are not used, so there is no code table to maintain.
  • Vietnam only, amounts in VND only.
  • GHN limits: 50,000 g per order, 200 cm per side, cash on delivery up to 50,000,000 VND. A declared value above 5,000,000 VND is sent as 5,000,000 (GHN’s maximum for insurance).
  • A parcel without dimensions is sent as 10 × 10 × 10 cm; GHN re-weighs and may change the fee.
  • Cash on delivery: GHN collects and pays the shop directly; the money never passes through Autoxide. GHN has no statement API in its public documentation, so reconcile by importing GHN’s statement (POST /api/v1/shipping/cod/statements).
  • Pickups of returned goods from a buyer are not booked through the connector (ghn.direction_unsupported).
  • Tracking by polling returns the current status only; the full journey comes from the webhook.

Error codes

CodeMeaning
ghn.account_incompleteThe carrier account has no token or shop_id
ghn.setting_invalidAn optional setting of the account has a value GHN does not accept
ghn.shop_not_foundThe token does not manage the shop, or the shop is locked
ghn.permission_missingGHN answered 403: the account lacks a permission; contact GHN
ghn.currency_unsupportedThe amount is not in VND
ghn.country_unsupportedThe address is outside Vietnam
ghn.service_unknownservice_code is not 2 or 5
ghn.direction_unsupportedReturn pickups are not supported
ghn.phone_invalidGHN refused a phone number
ghn.address_not_recognizedGHN does not recognise the province or ward name
ghn.route_not_supportedGHN does not serve the route with the chosen service
ghn.order_not_foundGHN has no such order in the account
ghn.webhook_bodyA callback body is not GHN’s JSON
shipping.carrier_errorAny other refusal; message carries GHN’s reason

Not verified yet

These follow the documentation where it is not explicit, and need a run with a real account:

  • Quotes use GHN’s order preview with a placeholder recipient (Quote, 0900000000).
  • Province and ward names are sent as the address module writes them (for example “Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh”); GHN’s catalogue lists short canonical names plus variants.
  • The label page is passed through as GHN serves it (PDF when the file is a PDF, otherwise HTML).
  • GHN documents no rate limit.

Taking payments with MoMo

MoMo is an e-wallet in Vietnam. With the momo adapter, a payment created in Autoxide gets a MoMo payment page (and a QR code) for the buyer, and is confirmed by itself when MoMo reports the result. The money goes from the buyer to your own MoMo business account; Autoxide never holds it.

Vietnamese: momo.vi.md.

Experimental. This adapter was written from the provider’s public documentation; not yet verified against the live service. Try it with MoMo’s sandbox, then with a small real payment, before relying on it. It uses MoMo’s Payment Gateway API v2 (captureWallet).

Each tenant connects its own MoMo account. Nothing here is a server-wide account, and the keys you store are encrypted and never shown again.

Before you start

  • The server operator turns the module on: AUTOXIDE_MODULES=official,momo (see docs/MODULES.md).
  • The server operator sets AUTOXIDE_HTTP_PUBLIC_URL to the address at which the internet reaches the API (https://…). MoMo sends payment results to that address.
  • You have a MoMo business account. In the MoMo for Business portal (business.momo.vn), the integration page shows three values: Partner Code, Access Key and Secret Key. The sandbox and the production environment each have their own set.

1. Store your MoMo account

You need the permission kernel.settings.manage.

curl -X PUT "$API/api/v1/kernel/settings/momo.connection.account.partner_code" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"value": "<Partner Code>"}'

curl -X PUT "$API/api/v1/kernel/settings/momo.connection.account.access_key" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"value": "<Access Key>"}'

curl -X PUT "$API/api/v1/kernel/settings/momo.connection.account.secret_key" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"value": "<Secret Key>"}'

# Test it: Autoxide asks MoMo about a payment that does not exist. MoMo answers "not found" when it
# accepts your keys.
curl -X POST "$API/api/v1/kernel/settings/momo.connection.account.secret_key/test" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
SettingRequiredWhat it is
momo.connection.account.partner_codeyesPartner Code of your MoMo business account.
momo.connection.account.access_keyyesAccess Key. Stored encrypted, never returned.
momo.connection.account.secret_keyyesSecret Key: signs every request and checks every notification. Stored encrypted, never returned.
momo.connection.account.environmentnoproduction (default) or sandbox. Use sandbox with MoMo’s test keys: no real money moves.
momo.connection.account.return_urlnoPage of your website the buyer returns to after paying, used when a payment has no return URL of its own.

The two keys are secrets: set them over REST as above. The MCP tool kernel.set_setting refuses secrets, so a key never passes through an AI agent.

2. The notification address — nothing to paste

MoMo calls this “IPN”. Autoxide sends your own notification address to MoMo with every payment it creates, so there is nothing to configure at MoMo. You can see the address (its last part identifies your tenant and cannot be guessed):

curl "$API/api/v1/kernel/connections/webhooks" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Look for the line momo.connection.account. Every notification is checked with your Secret Key before anything is recorded; a notification signed with another key is refused with payment.signature_invalid. MoMo may send the same notification several times; it is recorded once.

3. Take a payment

Create a payment with the partner momo and the method wallet, for example with POST /api/v1/ledger/payments (permission ledger.payments_create), or through a module that takes payments for you (orders, bookings…). The answer has:

  • checkout_url — MoMo’s payment page. Send the buyer there.
  • qr_payload — the QR code content, when MoMo returns one for your account.

When the buyer has paid, MoMo notifies Autoxide and the payment becomes succeeded. If MoMo reports a different amount than the payment asked for, nothing is booked: the payment becomes needs_review and waits for a person in the reconciliation queue.

Limits from MoMo’s documentation: VND only, 1,000 to 50,000,000 VND per wallet payment.

4. Refunds

Refund a payment as usual (POST /api/v1/ledger/payments/{id}/refunds). Full and partial refunds are sent to MoMo and the answer is final at once.

Error codes

CodeMeaningWhat to do
provider.not_configuredA required setting of step 1 is missing.Set it; the message names it.
momo.account_rejectedMoMo refused your keys (its result codes 11 and 13).Check the three values and the environment.
momo.return_url_requiredMoMo needs a return page.Send return_url with the payment, or set momo.connection.account.return_url.
orders.return_url_not_allowed (orders), or the field error ledger.return_url_not_allowed (POST /api/v1/ledger/payments)The return_url sent is not one of your shop’s addresses.Use an https:// address on a verified domain, or list its origin in ledger.payments.return_origins (see the shop guide).
momo.amount_out_of_rangeOutside 1,000–50,000,000 VND.Use another payment method.
momo.currency_not_supportedNot VND.Charge in VND.
momo.order_already_createdAn earlier attempt already reached MoMo, and MoMo does not hand out the payment link again.Create a new payment with a new reference.
momo.refund_already_sentAn earlier attempt of this refund already reached MoMo; it was not sent again.Check the refund in the MoMo for Business portal.
payment.provider_rejectedMoMo refused; the message has MoMo’s result code.See MoMo’s list of result codes.
payment.provider_unavailableMoMo did not answer, or is busy.Try again later.
public_url_missingThe server has no public address.The operator sets AUTOXIDE_HTTP_PUBLIC_URL.

What is not covered yet

  • Other MoMo products: ATM and credit cards through MoMo, pay later, recurring payments, payouts.
  • Statements: MoMo’s payment API has none, so reconciliation by statement (POST /api/v1/ledger/reconciliations) answers payment.not_supported for momo. Compare with the reports of the MoMo for Business portal.

For operators

VariableDefaultWhat it is
AUTOXIDE_MOMO_API_URLhttps://payment.momo.vnMoMo’s production API.
AUTOXIDE_MOMO_SANDBOX_API_URLhttps://test-payment.momo.vnMoMo’s sandbox API, for tenants with environment = sandbox.

Sources: MoMo’s developer site, https://developers.momo.vn/v3/docs/payment/api/wallet/onetime/, and MoMo’s official samples, https://github.com/momo-wallet/payment (read on 2026-11-21).

Security and performance test, November 2026

Vietnamese: README.vi.md.

What this is: a test of a running Autoxide server carried out by AI agents for the maintainers, before 1.0. Every number and finding below comes from requests that were actually sent to a release build on one cloud machine. It is not an audit by an independent third party and does not certify that Autoxide is free of vulnerabilities or meets any performance target. To report a problem, see SECURITY.md.

  • Date: 2026-11-25
  • Version tested: main at commit 8e6c78b7 (0.19.x), release build; the SCIM group again at f4d51628 (#515)
  • Roadmap item: step 70, P6 / P9; fixes tracked in P16 / P17 (docs/ROADMAP.md)
  • Earlier work this builds on: the November 2026 review (code review and black-box test, P14). This round went into what that report lists as not covered and re-tested what it lists as fixed.
  • Decision: D-20261125-pentest-scripts (where the scripts live, what the matrix holds)

Summary

  • 29,566 test cases run (14,783 on SQLite, 14,783 on PostgreSQL), generated from docs/openapi.json (1,319 operations) and docs/mcp-tools.json (312 tools) crossed with attack classes, plus hand-written cases for the areas below. Each case is one row of matrix.csv.gz.
  • No high or critical finding. No case let one tenant read or change another tenant’s data, and none moved money.
  • 3 medium findings: privilege escalation through SCIM group mappings (PT-1, fixed in #515 during this round and confirmed closed), the per-address SMS limit bypassed with IPv6 addresses behind a proxy (PT-4), and a slow-query problem in an off-by-default public feature (PT-15, open).
  • 9 low and 7 informational findings. Three findings (PT-15 to PT-17) came from the performance measurements, not from an attack.
  • Performance: about 1,700 (SQLite) / 2,400 (PostgreSQL) authenticated reads per second on a small cloud VM with the load generator on the same machine; no memory growth in 15-minute soaks; no request lost to SQLite lock contention; start in 1.1 s on a database of more than 1.3 million rows.

Scope and method

What was attacked

One server per database, built and run on the test machine, listening on 127.0.0.1 only:

  • cargo build --release -p autoxide (and, for the performance data set, the same build with --features bench-seed, which only adds the seeding commands);
  • AUTOXIDE_TENANCY_MODE=multi, AUTOXIDE_MODULES=all (official and experimental modules), event stream and metrics on, random secrets per run;
  • the general per-address rate limit turned off so scans were not cut short — sign-in throttling, SMS limits and other per-account limits stayed on, since they were under test;
  • no outside service: every provider address (eSMS, SePay, MoMo, GHN, SePay eInvoice) pointed at a local fake (scripts/fake_provider.py) that logs each request, which is how SMS codes were read; no AI provider; mail written to files. No request went to a host outside the machine.

Each server has a platform tenant and two tenants, a and b, each with an administrator, a staff account with a narrow role (read products, write own content, post comments, upload files), a customer (shop) account, a narrow API key and a broad one, an organization tree (root → north → north-1, root → south) with unit-scoped staff, and records created in every module by posting a body built from the OpenAPI schema of each POST operation. Record ids of each tenant were then collected from every list endpoint and used as attack inputs.

How cases were generated

GroupWhat each case doesGenerated from
AUTHNa protected operation called without a credentialevery operation with security
PERMan operation called by an actor lacking its x-permissions (customer, narrow staff, narrow API key), path filled with the actor’s own tenant’s idsevery operation with x-permissions
IDORan operation with a path id called by tenant a’s administrator with ids of tenant bevery operation with a path parameter
MCPAUTH / MCPPERM / MCPIDORthe same three for MCP tools/callevery tool in mcp-tools.json
INPUTSQL / template injection, NUL and right-to-left characters, 5,000-character values in every query parameter of every list endpoint; forged and cross-tenant cursors; mass assignment (tenant_id, id, created_by), arrays, 5,000-deep nesting, truncated JSON and wrong types in the body of every JSON writelist endpoints and write operations
TOKENforged access tokens (alg: none, stripped or empty-key signatures, HS512, swapped claims, extended exp, kid traversal), other tenant’s tokens and keys, refresh rotation, reuse and 20 concurrent refreshes, logout, disabled accounts, API key revocation, IP fences and spoofed client-address headers, sign-in lockout with case / space variants and spoofed headershand-written
SCIMwhat a SCIM token made by a non-administrator can reach, before and after the fix of PT-1; filter injection and nesting; paging limitshand-written
OTP / OTPXFFphone sign-in codes: reuse, wrong-code lock, cross-tenant and cross-number use, per-number and per-address limits — the latter also behind a simulated reverse proxy with IPv4 and IPv6 rotationhand-written
BIZpoint-of-sale sums near i64::MAX, zero / negative / foreign-currency payments, quantities, the same sale reference 10× at once, 12 concurrent sales of the last unit, idempotency keys (replay, other body, other tenant, 10 concurrent)hand-written
SSRFinternal, link-local, IPv6, encoded-IPv4, file: and gopher: addresses in every field that takes a URL; a local listener to catch any request; outside sites in return_url-like fieldsfields named *url*, endpoint, issuer in the OpenAPI document
PUBLICdrafts through public lists, search, feed, sitemap and slug; forged preview tokens; forged newsletter tokens; editing and deleting someone else’s commenthand-written
OPSsecurity headers, CORS from unknown origins, unauthenticated endpoints, error bodies, secrets in the server log, the request loghand-written
DOS50 MiB body, gzip bomb, 200,000-key object, 20,000 query parameters, limit=100000, wildcard search, 400 half-sent headers, 2,000 silent connections, 40 event streams for one user, 800 concurrent writes — each while checking that a normal request still answershand-written

The generated groups are mechanical by design: they prove that a rule holds everywhere, not that a clever attack fails. The hand-written groups are where the findings came from.

Two AI agents first read the code of the areas the earlier review had not covered (SCIM, phone verification, archive formats, loyalty / referral / point of sale, content / media / newsletter / analytics, MCP and REST parity, cursors) and returned hypotheses. Every hypothesis was tested against the running server before being reported; those that did not reproduce are listed as not confirmed (one was first rated high and turned out to be documented behaviour: PT-9).

Verdicts

pass — the server did what the case expected. fail — it did not, and the row names the finding. info — the behaviour is worth recording but is not a weakness (a documented exception, defaults returned for an unknown id, a documentation gap). not_run — the case could not run (for example tenant b had no record reachable from a list endpoint for that path, or the feature needs a provider this set-up does not have); the reason is in the row. Raw machine verdicts were checked by hand; the matrix keeps both (raw_verdict, verdict) and the rule that changed one is in scripts/summary.py.

The generated groups dominate the count (INPUT alone is more than half); the hand-written groups are small and are where every finding came from. The -xff runs (the SMS limit behind a proxy) are counted under their database. The SCIM re-run on the fixed commit (-main, 72 cases) is counted too.

not_run rows: IDOR and MCPIDOR cases for paths whose records tenant b did not have (the seeding posts one minimal body per operation, so nested records such as an order’s return or a shipment’s parcel often did not exist), identity verification (return_url of KYC, the L-11 item) because no identity provider is set up — L-11 is therefore neither confirmed nor cleared by this round.

Findings

Severity uses the scale of the November 2026 review: high lets an attacker act on data or money that is not theirs or take over an account under realistic conditions; medium is a real weakness that needs an extra condition (a specific permission, a configuration, a race); low / info is defence in depth. Every finding below was reproduced at least twice, on SQLite and on PostgreSQL, unless the row says otherwise; the script that reproduces it is named. The test team does not change code; the maintainers fixed most findings after the round — see Status of the findings for where each one stands. The script for PT-1 to PT-3 (SCIM privilege checks) is not published; its cases stay in the matrix.

No finding is high or critical. No case let tenant A read or change tenant B’s data, and none moved money.

IDSeverityAreaFindingReproduce
PT-1Mediumauth (SCIM)A SCIM token made by a user who holds only auth.scim.manage could create an account and add it to a SCIM group that the owner had mapped to the admin role; the account became an administrator. Claiming accounts and changing active / email already checked that the token’s creator covers the account (D-20261121-scim-claim-covers); the group path did not. Fixed in #515 (f4d51628); re-run on that commit on both databases: refused with 403, and none of five detours (several ops in one PATCH, replacing the member list, members inside the value, PUT of the group, a new group with the same name) gives the role.manual (script not published)
PT-4Mediumcompliance, bookingsBehind a reverse proxy (AUTOXIDE_HTTP_CLIENT_IP_HEADER set), the per-address limit on SMS codes is keyed on the full client address. Rotating IPv6 addresses inside one /64 sent 30 of 30 codes to 30 numbers through POST /api/v1/auth/phone/codes and POST /api/v1/bookings/public/phone-codes (each SMS paid by the shop); the same requests from one address are cut at 20. auth’s own phone sign-up limit already uses the /64 prefix. Same class as P-2 of the black-box test.scripts/otp.py … xff
PT-15MediumcontentPublic search can be slow on very large tables when the (off-by-default) feature is enabled; per-client limits do not fully bound the cost. Open.—
PT-2Lowauth (SCIM)DELETE /api/v1/auth/scim/v2/Users/{id} deleted an account the token’s creator does not cover, while PATCH … active=false on the same account was refused. Fixed in #515, confirmed: 403, the account stays.manual (script not published)
PT-3Lowauth (SCIM)DELETE /api/v1/auth/scim/group-mappings/{id} removed a mapping to a role the caller could not have created. Fixed in #515, confirmed: 403 auth.role_beyond_you.manual (script not published)
PT-5Loworders (POS)POST /api/v1/orders/pos/sales adds payment amounts (and change) with an unchecked sum; amounts near i64::MAX overflow, the handler panics (attempt to add with overflow, release builds keep overflow checks) and the request is answered 500. The server keeps running. Needs orders.pos.sell.scripts/business.py
PT-6Loworders (POS)The currency of each POS payment is ignored: a payment sent as {"amount":"150000","currency":"JPY"} (or USD) settles a VND sale and is recorded as VND.scripts/business.py
PT-7LowcomplianceTen wrong codes across the challenges of one phone number block new sign-in codes for that number for 24 hours (compliance.otp_daily_limit). A stranger can lock someone out of SMS sign-in for a day at the cost of two SMS.scripts/otp.py
PT-8LowseveralRecords created by a tenant-wide caller accept an org_id (or role_id) that is not a unit (role) of the tenant — a random id, or another tenant’s id: catalog products, menus, catalog imports, POS shifts, sandboxes, settings keyed by unit. Nothing of the other tenant is read or changed (the record stays in the caller’s tenant, and unit-scoped callers are refused with org_out_of_scope), but the record points at a unit that does not exist.scripts/mcp.py (MCPIDOR), scripts/authz.py
PT-9LowauthPUT /api/v1/auth/users/{id}/roles and the tool auth.set_user_roles give any role, including admin, without the “only grant what you hold” check that PUT /api/v1/auth/users/{id}/memberships makes (more_than_you_have). auth.roles.manage is documented as admin-equivalent and cannot be scoped to a unit, so this is an inconsistency rather than an escalation; a subagent’s first report rated it high, which reproduction did not support.manual, see the matrix
PT-16LowcontentCreating an entry checks free slugs with slug = $x OR slug LIKE '$x-%'. Under PostgreSQL with a non-C collation the unique index cannot answer the LIKE, so every create runs a parallel sequential scan of the tenant’s entries (100,000 rows: 50 ms alone, 9–22 creates a second under load against about 75 on SQLite). Two drafts with the same title created at the same moment can also pick the same slug; one gets 409 instead of the next suffix (seen 12 times in 8 concurrent streams, PostgreSQL only — SQLite serializes writes).scripts/perf.py, EXPLAIN ANALYZE in this report
PT-17LowHTTP serverOn PostgreSQL, after SIGTERM under load the server logs stopped at once but the process stays alive another 30–132 s (three runs); without load, or on SQLite, it exits in under a second. A supervisor that waits for the process (systemd, Kubernetes before its kill timeout) waits that long. Cause not found in this round.scripts/perf.sh
PT-10InfonotificationsA push subscription accepts any https endpoint, including loopback, link-local (169.254.169.254) and private addresses, from any signed-in user (buyers included). No web push sender ships in this repository, so nothing fetches it today; the WebPushSender contract should require the public-address filter before one does.scripts/ssrf.py
PT-11InfocontentPublic taxonomy reads can expose terms that no published entry uses yet (info, open).—
PT-12InfoanalyticsPublic analytics ingestion can be polluted by non-browser clients (info, open).—
PT-13InfoOpenAPIA few x-permissions lists are narrower than what the service accepts (listing banners also accepts content.read); the matrix flagged them as “allowed without the permission”. Documentation, not a bypass.scripts/authz.py
PT-14InfoHTTPAbout 210 operations answer 428 (If-Match missing), 422 or 404 before the permission check, so an unauthorised caller learns that the endpoint wants an ETag or which fields are wrong. No data is returned.scripts/authz.py
PT-18InfonewsletterThe per-mailbox cap on newsletter confirmation mails can be stretched (info, open).—
PT-19Infoauth (SCIM)A SCIM token may still alter non-privilege link metadata of accounts outside its creator’s scope; not re-tested.—

Hypotheses checked and not confirmed: refresh-token races (20 concurrent refreshes, one success), forged cursors (server-chosen column, values bound), SCIM filter injection and nesting, OTP brute force (5 tries per code, codes bound to number and tenant), per-address SMS limits without a trusted proxy (spoofed X-Forwarded-For is ignored), payment return_url (P-5 holds), webhook targets on internal addresses (refused, and nothing reached the local listener), CSV formula injection (guarded in the shared writer), deleting another tenant’s comment (the endpoint answers deleted: true without saying whether it saw the comment, and the comment stays), archive traversal (no archive format is parsed: exports are JSONL written by the server).

Status of the findings

As of main at 9b7d1a6d (2026-11-26), from the roadmap (step 70, P16 and P17) and the pull requests that closed them. Only PT-1 to PT-3 were re-tested by this team after the fix; the other fixes carry their own tests.

Performance

Set-up

  • Machine: a small cloud VM; server, database and load generator on the same machine, so every number is a lower bound and a comparison point, not a commitment.
  • Build: release, Rust 1.100.0; SQLite bundled with libsqlite3-sys 0.40 (file on local disk, WAL); PostgreSQL 16.15 as installed, not tuned.
  • Load generator: oha 1.17.0, 10 seconds per scenario.
  • Data: scripts/bench-seed.sh full of the repository: 5,000 users, 50,000 images with derived copies, 100,000 published posts in two languages (20 categories, 200 tags, 50 authors), 1,000,000 published comments. Seeding took 205 s on SQLite and 220 s on PostgreSQL.
  • Rate limiting off, log level warn, access tokens valid for a day.

Breaking point

Reads (GET /auth/me) and writes (PATCH /auth/users/{id}, one row and an event) ramped to 1,024 connections:

ConnectionsRead SQLiteRead PostgreSQLWrite SQLiteWrite PostgreSQL
2561,522 req/s, p99 213 ms2,353 req/s, p99 131 ms776 req/s, p99 1.3 s812 req/s, p99 1.3 s
5121,540 req/s, p99 1.3 s2,340 req/s, p99 1.2 s810 req/s, p99 1.8 s846 req/s, p99 1.6 s
1,0241,576 req/s, p99 1.6 s2,368 req/s, p99 1.4 s819 req/s, p99 3.4 s855 req/s, p99 3.2 s

Throughput stays flat past 32–64 connections (the 4 CPUs are saturated; latency grows with the queue) and every request still succeeded: no 5xx, no SQLite busy error, no dropped connection. The machine, not the server, is the limit at this size.

Lifecycle and soak

  • Startup on the seeded database (process start to /health/ready): 1.12 s on both databases.
  • Graceful shutdown under 64 connections: SQLite exited 0.27–0.34 s after SIGTERM with no error. PostgreSQL logged stopped at once but the process stayed alive 30–132 s (three runs: 98 s, 132 s, 30 s); without load it exits in under a second (PT-17).
  • Soak, 15 minutes of mixed reads, lists, public pages, MCP calls and rate-limited writes: SQLite 706,174 requests, PostgreSQL 967,029, all successful; peak resident memory of the first and second half 385 → 389 MiB (+0.9 %) and 343.5 → 343.6 MiB (+0.0 %); open files flat. No leak seen.

Queries

  • N+1: statements per request were counted on PostgreSQL with log_min_duration_statement = 0 and an API-only process (scripts/querycount.py). The count does not grow with the page size (public posts: 11 statements for 20 and for 50 posts; GET /content/entries?limit=50: 7; GET /auth/me: 4). No N+1 found on the paths measured.
  • Deep pages: walking 400 pages of 100 entries (40,000 rows) costs about the same per page at the end as at the start (cursor pagination, no OFFSET); the worst page was 91 ms (PostgreSQL) / 86 ms (SQLite), the first page with a cold cache.
  • Full scans found: the slug check when creating an entry (slug = $x OR slug LIKE '$x-%', which PostgreSQL cannot answer from the unique index under a non-C collation, so it runs a parallel sequential scan of every entry — PT-16; EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 33,334 rows removed by each of the three workers).
  • Idle load: a process with the default role all runs about 80 SQL statements per second on PostgreSQL while no request comes in (each module’s outbox and job pollers). Not a problem at this size; it is the floor of database load per worker process.
  • The roadmap already plans to replace about 140 unpaginated list endpoints (P9). This round did not re-measure them one by one; the largest lists measured here (users, entries, media, audit, comments) are all paginated and indexed.

Limits of this round

  • Done by AI agents, with the scripts in this directory; not a replacement for testing by an independent party, nor for testing with real provider accounts (payments, SMS, carriers and identity verification were all fakes).
  • One machine: the load generator competes with the server for CPU. Use the numbers to compare before and after a change on the same machine.
  • Tested at 8e6c78b7: the “resting” mode for turned-off modules (#514) and the move of list endpoints to Page<T> (P9) landed after it and are not covered.
  • Not covered: passkeys and OpenID Connect end to end (they need a browser and a real identity provider), payment and carrier webhooks with real signatures from real providers, WebSockets beyond the per-user cap, file and media uploads at their size limits, tenant move / relocation between databases under load, the per-tenant dedicated database placement, ai with a real model.
  • The generated groups use one minimal body per operation: a write whose validation needs related records (an order return, a shipment parcel) usually stopped at validation, so authorization after validation was not reached for those (PT-14 counts them).

Reproducing

Everything runs on one machine with Python 3 (standard library), curl, oha and, for PostgreSQL, a local server:

cargo build --release -p autoxide
cd docs/security/pentest-2026-11/scripts
./all.sh sqlite   /tmp/px/sqlite   18080
./all.sh postgres /tmp/px/postgres 18081 postgres://postgres:<password>@127.0.0.1:5432/<empty database>
python3 summary.py                      # matrix.csv(.gz) and the tables above

cargo build --release -p autoxide --features bench-seed
AUTOXIDE_BIN=../../../../target/release/autoxide PERF_SOAK=15m ./perf.sh sqlite /tmp/px/perf 18090
python3 perf_tables.py

Raw results go to results/ (not committed). The behind-a-proxy SMS case needs its own server; the command is at the end of all.sh. A finding’s script reproduces it while the finding is open; once it is fixed, the fix adds a Rust test on both databases and the script case turns to pass.

RC trial, round 1 (AI agents playing users)

English · Tiếng Việt

Important: the testers were AI agents playing a role, not people. Round 1 ran on main at version 0.19.0 (before 1.0.0-rc.1), as an early check (the project owner asked AI agents to play users before outside testers, in a few rounds). Every tester saw only public documents (README, docs/guides, docs/*.md, OpenAPI, examples/), never the source of crates/ or modules/ (the module-author role could also read modules/<name>/src/api.rs). Subagents: the newcomer role ran on a small model (to imitate a less experienced person), the other four on a mid-size model. No real secret and no real provider or AI model was used.

Environment limits that shaped the results (not product bugs): 4 CPU cores, no Docker daemon (the Docker quickstart was not tried), so every role used the binary, with SQLite or a local PostgreSQL 16. The binary was built once up front (cargo build -p autoxide, debug, 10 min 06 s on a cold cache); roles timed themselves from “binary exists”. Timings below come from the agents’ own clocks and are approximate where stated.

Numbers for G9 (agent playing a role, not a person)

MeasureResultReading
Minutes to the first request that returns data (binary already built, .env written)under 1 minute (36 s from migrate to a data request)Does not count reading the docs, writing .env, or building. Building from source took 10 min 06 s (debug, cold). Quickstart with Docker not measured. G9’s “under 5 minutes from download” cannot be judged until a prebuilt binary or a working image path is measured.
Minutes to the first module (generate, build, run an endpoint)about 33 min, of which 32 min 08 s was compiling the core into the module’s own target directoryThe build was slowed by a stray second build on the same 4-core machine, so a clean run is faster but not measured. Generate: 23 s. From a finished binary to a working endpoint: about 1 minute. G9’s “under 30 minutes” is at risk on a cold build unless the guide offers a prebuilt option.

Goal: README to first request, then “ask an AI” to add a small feature. Result: part 1 reached; part 2 not reached (the module build did not finish in 26 minutes: the machine was loaded by other roles, see role 2).

Role 2 — Module author outside the repository

Goal: follow docs/guides/writing-a-module.md, make a small module in a directory outside the repo, run check-module, test on SQLite and PostgreSQL. Result: reached. The module links was generated with cargo xtask new-module --external … links link --core-path … (the guide’s way); it is a renamed copy of the sample, the tester did not write new business logic. check-module: no violations. Tests: 8 + 4 pass on SQLite and on PostgreSQL (port 15432). POST / GET /api/v1/links work, a duplicate gives 409 links.url_taken.

Time: generate 0:23; first server build 32:08 (compile wait, slowed by a stray build); binary to a working endpoint about 1:00; check-module 1 s when the machine is free; SQLite tests 6:41 (rebuild after a machine restart), PostgreSQL 10 s.

Role 3 — Connecting an AI agent (MCP)

Goal: connect over MCP with an API key, list tools, do three multi-step jobs, note tools whose description is not enough. Result: partly reached (about 4 min, no build). Done: content (draft, search, update, revisions, review request); catalog + draft invoice (tax line computed correctly); pagination and filters (three pages, 3+3+1, correct). Not done: customer, product, draft order (no tools for it; see UT-5).

Real bugs:

  • An authorization scope problem in API-key management over MCP (reported privately; details withheld until it is fixed and then published).
  • catalog.create_product accepts "tax_category":"nope" and stores it (the description says it must be in GET /api/v1/tax/categories).
  • catalog.list_products readiness:"x", audit.list_entries module:"nope" or subject:"bad" return an empty list instead of an error (a wrong status does report one): inconsistent.
  • Audit entries of an agent show actor_kind:"user" with actor_api_key_id, no key name; mcp.md says “under the key’s name”.

Role 4 — Operator

Goal: set up with PostgreSQL 16 (no Docker daemon), migrate, doctor, metrics, backup, restore, graceful stop, upgrade. Result: reached (4 min 16 s). All documented commands that could run did what the docs say. Restore: 460 tables, row counts match (apart from rows the tester added by logging in), the old admin password works, 3355 address units and 8 tax rates are intact. Not tried (no Docker, out of scope): docker compose / docker run, gh attestation verify, systemd, SQLite→PostgreSQL copy, multi-tenant, OTLP, encrypted backup / PITR.

Upgrade: no earlier release to upgrade from. Simulated the documented module on/off path: serve warns modules_turned_off, doctor warns, autoxide modules says “1 table(s) with rows”, backup refuses with instructions; migrate down customers then up is clean.

Role 5 — Shop owner using the API (curl and the TypeScript SDK)

Goal: customer, product, stock, promotion, order, simulated payment, draft e-invoice. Result: partly reached. The whole sale flow ran with curl and with the SDK; money checked by hand (300,000; 480,000 with tax 43,636; 210,000 with tax 19,091), integer strings plus VND; four buyers in parallel for the last item gave exactly one order; partial refund, cancel of a paid order and refund replays did not double. About 15 min (estimate); about 6.5 min of it was looking for steps the guide lacks. The SDK runs directly with Node 22, no npm install.

Real bugs:

  • L1 (most serious): stock on_hand never goes down after delivery. Sandbox tenant, one variant with 10 in stock, order 2, pay (notification), create a shipment, POST /shipping/shipments/{id}/status through ready_to_ship, picked_up, in_transit, delivered (or POST /orders/{id}/transitions to preparing, shipping, delivered). Seen after waiting 20 s: order delivered, but GET /inventory/levels shows on_hand 10, available 8, reserved 2; GET /inventory/movements has only the +10 adjustment, no sale; the reservation stays confirmed; the order’s fulfillment_status stays unfulfilled. Expected (INVENTORY.md, Reservations: “fulfil — writes sale lines”): sale −2, on_hand 8, reserved 0, fulfilled. available is right, so no overselling, but the ledger of stock is wrong.
  • L2: payment_actions[].payment_id from checkout (and from POST /orders/{id}/payment-link) is not the ledger payment id: GET /ledger/payments/{id} returns 404 ledger.payment_not_found; the real id appears only in GET /ledger/payments (filter source_id).
  • L3 (small): repeating checkout, or cancelling a guest order, with the same Idempotency-Key returns 200 (first call 201) without the Idempotent-Replayed: true header, unlike retries.md and the OpenAPI text.
  • L4 (small): POST /orders/{id}/payment-link after a failed first payment returns the first (failed) payment_id and status_token; that token stays pending while the ledger has a new payment with another id.
  • L5 (small): a MoMo notification with the wrong amount sets needs_review (as documented); a correct notification sent afterwards does not bring it to succeeded and the order stays pending_payment; nothing says how an operator clears it.

Summary by priority

  1. Blocking for 1.0: UT-1 (stock never decreases on delivery), UT-2 (API-key scope problem over MCP, details withheld).
  2. Annoying, fix before the RC feedback window: UT-3 (fastest path without Docker: binary, secrets, migrate up, port, PostgreSQL), UT-4 (no way to try a sale without real providers; shop guide missing steps), UT-5 (MCP tools: missing parameter descriptions, price lists / customers, validation of values), UT-6 (payment ids, idempotency headers, payment-link replay), UT-7 (first build time of a module outside the repo).
  3. Small: UT-8 (messages and logs for operators), UT-9 (rate-limit docs vs behaviour, internal id in public data).

Note: the first-build time of a module (about 30 min) puts G9’s “first module under 30 minutes” at risk.

Housekeeping: a second build left running by role 1 competed with role 2 for CPU for most of its wait; it could not be stopped from this session. Files left in /tmp of the trial machine only; nothing was changed in the product code. Role 4 and role 2 left a local PostgreSQL running (ports 15434 and 15432).

  • PUT /api/v1/conversations/voice/lines/{org_id}: Set the phone line of a unit.
  • POST /api/v1/conversations/voice/webhooks/{provider}/{line_token}: Receive a call status notification from the voice provider.

  • PUT /api/v1/customers/me/wishlist/alerts: Turn wishlist alerts on or off.
  • POST /api/v1/customers/me/wishlist/merge: Merge the wishlist kept in the browser into your account.
  • DELETE /api/v1/customers/me/wishlist/{product_id}: Remove a product (all its variants) from your wishlist.
  • GET /api/v1/customers/referral-rules: List referral reward rules, newest first.
  • POST /api/v1/customers/referral-rules: Set referral rewards.
  • GET /api/v1/customers/reminder-rules: List abandoned cart reminder rules, newest first.
  • POST /api/v1/customers/reminder-rules: Set abandoned cart reminders.
  • GET /api/v1/customers/{id}: Get a customer.

  • POST /api/v1/customers/{id}/store-credit/adjustments: Add or remove store credit of a customer.

  • PATCH /api/v1/forms/submissions/{id}: Change the status of a submission.
  • DELETE /api/v1/forms/{id}: Delete a form.

health

  • GET /: Where to start: name, version and links to the API description.
  • GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server: Authorization server metadata.

  • GET /health/ready: Readiness probe: can the service handle requests?

inventory

  • POST /api/v1/inventory/adjustments: Adjust stock in one warehouse, each line with a reason.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/adjustments/{id}: Get a stock adjustment with the ledger lines it wrote.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/counts: List stock counts in your scope.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/counts: Open a stock count in one warehouse.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/counts/{id}: Get a stock count with its lines.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/counts/{id}/apply: Apply a stock count: each difference becomes a count ledger line with its reason.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/counts/{id}/cancel: Cancel an open stock count.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/counts/{id}/import: Record counted quantities from a CSV file.
  • PUT /api/v1/inventory/counts/{id}/lines: Record counted quantities.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/levels: List stock levels (variant × warehouse) in your scope.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/levels/{id}: Get one stock level.
  • PATCH /api/v1/inventory/levels/{id}: Change the reorder point of a stock level.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/lots: List lots (with expiry dates) in your scope.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/movements: List the stock movement ledger in your scope.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/public/availability: Public availability of variants at stores.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/public/restock-alerts: Ask for a back-in-stock alert (public).
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/public/restock-alerts/confirm: Confirm a back-in-stock alert (public).
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/public/restock-alerts/stop: Stop a back-in-stock alert (public).
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/purchase-orders: List purchase orders in your scope.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/purchase-orders: Create a purchase order as a draft.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/purchase-orders/{id}: Get a purchase order.
  • PATCH /api/v1/inventory/purchase-orders/{id}: Change a draft purchase order (its lines are replaced).
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/purchase-orders/{id}/cancel: Cancel a purchase order that is a draft, or ordered with nothing received.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/purchase-orders/{id}/close: Close a purchase order: what has not arrived stops counting as incoming.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/purchase-orders/{id}/order: Send a draft purchase order to the supplier: its units count as incoming.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/receipts: List goods receipts in your scope.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/receipts: Receive goods into a warehouse, against a purchase order or directly.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/receipts/{id}: Get a goods receipt.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/receipts/{id}/retry-ledger: Post a receipt whose ledger posting failed again.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/reports/valuation: Value of the stock now: on hand × weighted average cost, per warehouse and currency.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/reservations: List stock reservations of orders sold by units in your scope.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/reservations/{id}/release: Release a stuck reservation by hand.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/settings/{org_id}: Get how a store picks warehouses.
  • PUT /api/v1/inventory/settings/{org_id}: Change how a store picks warehouses.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/sources/{selling_org_id}: List the warehouses serving a store or channel, in the order they are tried.
  • PUT /api/v1/inventory/sources/{selling_org_id}: Replace the warehouses serving a store or channel.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/supplier-returns: List supplier returns in your scope.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/supplier-returns: Return goods to a supplier.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/supplier-returns/{id}: Get a supplier return.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/suppliers: List suppliers in your scope with what you owe each one.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/suppliers: Create a supplier.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/suppliers/{id}: Get a supplier with what you owe it.
  • PATCH /api/v1/inventory/suppliers/{id}: Change a supplier.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/transfers: List stock transfers from or to warehouses in your scope.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/transfers: Create a stock transfer as a draft.
  • GET /api/v1/inventory/transfers/{id}: Get a stock transfer.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/transfers/{id}/cancel: Cancel a draft transfer.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/transfers/{id}/close: Close a transfer in transit: what has not arrived is written off from incoming.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/transfers/{id}/receive: Receive goods of a transfer in transit, all or part.
  • POST /api/v1/inventory/transfers/{id}/ship: Ship a draft transfer: the goods leave the source and are in transit.
